item.title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
item.dc:creator: Alex Iankoulski
item.description: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that pairs reasoning and tool use with multimodal understanding. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM.
item.content:encoded:
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Nano Omni, Super, Ultra, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS.

About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details:

  • 120B total parameters, 12B active per token.
  • Hybrid Mamba-2, MoE, and attention layers with a RADIO vision encoder.
  • Context length up to 1M tokens.
  • Input: text, image, document, and video.
  • Output: text.
  • BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints.

NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. (technical report)

Model architecture

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding.

Use cases

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding:

  • Coding: test and validate code, analyze errors, recommend fixes.
  • Web research: cross-reference and verify sources returned by search tools.
  • Document intelligence: read tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries.
  • Cyber security: identify vulnerabilities and triage threats.
  • Video understanding: search, content, review, and incident analysis.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit. For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog.

Minimum GPU configurations

vLLM (GPU Model / min count) BF16 NVFP4
B200/GB200 8 2
B300/GB300 4 1
H200 8 4
H100 16 8

Deployment on AWS

This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family.

Deployment architecture

The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. The following figure shows a standard Amazon EKS cluster.

Figure 1: Standard Amazon EKS cluster architecture for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models

NVIDIA Dynamo serves the model aggregated on a single node or disaggregated with prefill and decode on different nodes. For vision-language models, the image/video encoding stage can in addition run disaggregated on its own node.

Validation and performance

This architecture has been validated on both p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA B200 GPUs) and p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) instances. You can validate the cluster and its network with an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce micro-benchmark.

Figure 2: GPU and EFA utilization during an NCCL all-reduce validation test

Seeing utilization on all GPUs and traffic on all EFA adapters while the NCCL test is running, verifies that the cluster is working as expected.

You can measure the performance of a deployed model on the cluster with the NVIDIA aiperf tool.

Figure 3: aiperf performance metrics for the deployed model

The aiperf output in the upper left pane shows key performance indicators (KPIs) like time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput in tokens per second (TPS). By taking these measurements at various levels of concurrency, we can study how latency and throughput depend on the number of concurrent requests. This information is essential to thoughtfully plan capacity and model deployment topology. The aws-do-eks container provides automation for visualizing GPU and EFA utilization as well as running aiperf and concurrency sweeps with single commands.

Figure 4: Concurrency sweep comparing aggregated and disaggregated deployments

The preceding concurrency sweep diagram reveals that the inference of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has lower TTFT and about the same ITL between aggregated and disaggregated deployments on two nodes.

A chart like this is useful when making deployment decisions. Draw your latency budget as horizontal lines, for example TTFT under 600 ms (about 1 second) and ITL under 100 ms per token. The rightmost point under both lines is the throughput one replica of this topology can serve within the service level objective (SLO), here c32, or about 320 tokens per second. To plan capacity, divide your target tokens per second by this per-replica throughput and find the number of prefill-decode pairs to deploy. Re-running the same sweep after a change (precision, TP/PP shape, aggregated versus disaggregated, a new Dynamo or vLLM release) makes the trade-off visible immediately. A curve that moves right and down is a win. Because TTFT and ITL are plotted separately, it also tells you which side to scale: rising ITL says add decode capacity, and rising TTFT says add prefill capacity.

Conclusion

This post covers the architecture and performance evaluation patterns for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM. To get started, deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in your own account, using the reference implementation. More inference blueprints are also available in the AI on EKS project. To get further hands-on experience with inference on EKS, register for our upcoming workshops.

item.title: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Omar Elkharbotly
item.description: Stand up a governed, multi-account Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This post walks through the architecture and an open-source reference blueprint: the operating model, control plane, per-Workstream cells, separate inference and tool gateways, and a CI/CD evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before production.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve tried to get an agent into production, the model and tool use are not the blocker. The main bottleneck is everything around them: how many teams can build within a secure environment, which team owns each model and tool, how AgentOps and error handling stay inside a pre-defined boundary, and how platform, Workstream, and finance teams see cost and health across accounts. For a Platform team that wants to support many agentic use cases, that’s a platform product to design and operate. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Workstream teams. Workstream teams are the domain or product teams that build and own agents on the platform.

Each Workstream team needs a paved road with approved models and tools, short-lived workload identity, isolated runtime and memory, automated evaluation, rollback, telemetry, and cost attribution. These controls need to remain consistent as Workstream teams customize prompts, tools, data access, and application behavior. When every team assembles them, controls drift, shared services become a bottleneck, and ownership is difficult to audit.

In this post, we walk through the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover the multi-account operating model, the Platform control plane, a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern, separate inference and tool gateways, and an evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before promotion to production. By the end, you should be able to deploy a governed Workstream from the companion blueprint, validate its security and lifecycle contracts, and use it as the foundation for your own agentic AI platform in the organization.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular services for building, deploying, and operating agents at scale, including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations. The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint, built on AgentCore, adds the surrounding enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code: ownership, account boundaries, software delivery, observability, cost governance, and retirement.

Architectural principles

Before diving into the solution details, it helps to understand the organizational needs that drive the platform architecture. The common challenges we have heard from customers who establish an agent platform fall into these five categories:

  1. Governed model access: Every untrusted inference request must pass through an approved inference gateway. The gateway applies the organization’s guardrails (for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails or a third-party provider), restricts which models and inference AWS Regions each Workstream can use, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits, token quotas, and budgets so that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. It also carries workload identity and emits attribution data.
  2. Governed tool access: Agents must discover and invoke only approved tools through an authenticated Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, with exact targets, least-privilege execution roles, policy decisions, and an auditable owner.
  3. Delegated delivery: Workstream teams (for example, product teams) need to ship and roll back independently inside pre-approved boundaries, without waiting for the platform team to deploy each application or granting developers a direct infrastructure write path.
  4. Fleet operations and cost: Several personas need visibility across accounts without gaining write access to team workloads. Agent operations engineers need logs, metrics, traces, and quotas. Workstream owners need cost per agent against their budgets. FinOps and finance teams need chargeback by team or business unit through AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Security and governance leads need evidence of which workload called which model and tool.
  5. Bounded evidence and lifecycle: Every agent release needs proof at each boundary it touches:
    1. Model access: An approved model call succeeds, and a call to an unapproved model or Region is denied.
    2. Tool access: A subscribed tool call succeeds, and a call to a tool outside the agent’s subscription is denied with the expected error.
    3. Identity: A request from another workstream’s account or identity is rejected.
    4. Release: The previous agent runtime version can be restored.
    5. Retirement: Teardown removes the agent’s runtime, memory, tool gateway, and tool grants in dependency order, and confirms nothing is left behind.

The blueprint addresses these needs through four connected planes: developer experience, platform control, Workstream execution, and assurance and operations. The unit of scale is the Workstream cell, not a manually configured agent or one shared workload account. The blueprint README documents the responsibilities of each plane in detail. And you will read the main planes: Agentic AI Platform control plane and Repeatable Workstream cell in the later paragraphs.

Operating models and platform components

Enterprises usually adopt one of three operating models for agentic AI:

  • Centralized: A single artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) team builds and runs every agent. Governance is consistent, but that team quickly becomes a bottleneck as the number of use cases grows.
  • Decentralized: Each business unit builds and operates its own agents. Teams can move quickly, but without shared standards, controls tend to drift, effort gets duplicated, and cost visibility suffers.
  • Federated: A central Platform team provides shared, governed services while domain teams retain ownership of their agents, tools, and data. This model balances team autonomy with consistent guardrails and is where most enterprises land.
  • For assistance choosing, see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance page on Governance Models.

Following patterns we have observed in customer engagements, the blueprint implements the federated model. The Platform team is the hub, typically a Platform product manager, architect, platform engineers, agent operations engineers, and a security and governance lead. Workstream teams are the spokes, made up of agent developers, a domain tech lead, and AI/ML engineers. An executive sponsor and the CISO sit above both.

In this blueprint, the Platform team owns the definition of each component: templates, versions, policies, and admission. Each Workstream account runs its own instance of the per-team components (Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway), so a failure or rollback stays inside one team’s boundary.

Solution overview

This solution delivers a governed, multi-account Agentic AI Platform that platform teams operate, and workstream teams such as internal product and engineering teams consume through versioned, self-service interfaces.

At enterprise scale, the developer experience plane is a catalog of organization-approved, versioned agent templates. The blueprint ships reference templates for Strands, LangGraph, and CrewAI, but you can use your choice of framework when the template preserves the same inference gateway, tool gateway, identity, policy, evaluation, and delivery contracts. Application teams own prompts, agent logic, tools, and evaluation cases. The Platform team owns the common controls and release requirements.

Out of the four planes, two carry most of the architecture:

  1. Agentic AI Platform control plane: The Platform account publishes versioned templates and interfaces, operates AWS Agent Registry governance records and shared Inference Gateways, admits models and Guardrails, orchestrates reviewed releases, and aggregates fleet signals. Teams consume these capabilities through code, descriptors, and pipelines rather than administrator sessions or deployment tickets.
  2. Repeatable Workstream cell: Each product or domain receives an isolated boundary with a team-owned source repository, a Workload pipeline, and three Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities: AgentCore Runtime, actor-scoped AgentCore Memory, and an AgentCore Gateway that uses AWS_IAM authorization and exposes only the approved tool targets. The cell also holds local customer managed AWS KMS keys, tags, alarms, budgets, and a CloudWatch Observability Access Manager (OAM) source link. One cell can deploy, fail, roll back, or retire without coordinating with another team’s release.

Key components

The following diagram illustrates the operating model and governed flow of the solution.

Figure 1: Enterprise Agentic AI Platform operating model, showing the governance foundation, the Platform control plane, repeatable team-owned Workstream cells, and the software delivery, inference, tool, telemetry, and ownership flows between them.

The architecture consists of the following account layers:

  1. Management and governance foundation. AWS Organizations, AWS IAM Identity Center, preventive policy, audit, retention, and cost policy establish the enterprise boundary. These are logical responsibilities that can map to an existing AWS Control Tower landing zone rather than requiring a duplicate account structure.
  2. Security, audit, and observability layer. AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, log archive, and an Amazon CloudWatch OAM sink provide independent control-plane evidence and fleet visibility. Central operators can query shared signals without gaining write access to Workstream resources.
  3. Platform layer of Agentic AI Platform. Separate Platform environments own golden paths, the governance catalog, Guardrails, shared Inference Gateways, exact tool aliases, pipelines, compatibility, quotas, and common operational interfaces. Platform changes are tested against representative cells before wider rollout.
  4. Workstream fleet layer. Each product, domain, or regulated boundary receives one or more nonproduction and production cells. Teams own Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, tools, data, prompts, evaluation cases, application incidents, and service-level objectives (SLOs). The same baseline can be repeated across many cells while preserving account-level isolation.

Solution walkthrough

The following sections trace the key design decisions: account topology, preventive and detective controls, the AgentCore execution path, and the delivery pipeline.

Account topology and organizational units

The blueprint defines logical account roles that separate enterprise governance, shared Platform services, and team-owned execution:

Role Landing-zone placement Purpose
Management foundation Root / Security and Management Organizations, Identity Center, preventive policy, audit, retention, and cost policy
Security and log archive Security CloudTrail, AWS Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, and retained audit data
Observability Security or Operations CloudWatch OAM sink and fleet logs, metrics, traces, and cost views
Agentic AI Platform Agent Platform Golden paths, AWS Agent Registry, Guardrails, Inference Gateways, pipelines, and fleet controls
Workstream cell Agent Workstreams Team-owned Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, tools, data, evaluation, and application SLOs
Additional Workstream cells Agent Workstreams Repeat the same baseline per product, domain, environment, or regulated boundary

This topology integrates into an existing landing zone, a pre-configured, secure, and scalable multi-account AWS environment, where the Management, Platform, and Workstream labels describe responsibilities rather than a fixed three-account estate. An organization can operate multiple validated Platform environments and many Workstream account pairs. Start with one representative cell and prove onboarding, production promotion, rollback, centralized observability, and zero-residual retirement before repeating the baseline.

Service control policies

Service control policies constrain the maximum permissions available to Platform and Workstream accounts. They complement, rather than replace, IAM, gateway authorization, Guardrails, resource policies, network controls, and pipeline evidence. The blueprint renders and reviews the effective policies for the exact account and Region instead of relying on source-code intent alone.

  1. Model and Region admission: Organization policy and Gateway execution roles restrict inference to approved models and the supported Region. Adding a model or Region requires service availability, residency, IAM, quality, cost, rollback, observability, and denial validation.
  2. Guardrail and inference enforcement: Agents do not call model providers directly. Inference crosses the governed gateway, where the stage Guardrail and model allow-list are applied.
  3. Pipeline-only Workstream mutation: Workstream teams open pull requests and use the Workload pipeline. Direct developer deployment into Workstream accounts is outside the supported operating model, which keeps the reviewed release and evidence path non-bypassable.
  4. Registry and Gateway governance: Workstream Gateway synthesis fails when a subscribed Registry record is missing, changed, or not approved.
  5. Scoped deployment roles: Bootstrap policies are generated per account and Region, validated with AWS Identity and Access Management Access (IAM) Analyzer, and checked through effective-policy simulation. Administrator access is reserved for initial setup rather than routine pipeline execution.
  6. Separation of duties and adversarial proof: Platform controls model, Guardrail, Registry, and shared-service admission. Workstream teams control application behavior. Every denied path is paired with an authorized positive call and a mutation that proves the intended control caused the denial.

An administrator inside a Workstream account can’t create a supported fast path around these controls. New or changed organization policies need a sandbox or representative-cell soak, exact allow and deny tests, and a rollback plan before broad attachment.

CI/CD pipeline with evaluation gates

The blueprint uses reviewed Platform and Workload pipelines to enforce the following promotion sequence:

  1. Source and review: A pull request establishes the immutable source revision. The pipeline pins the intended branch so an unmerged change can’t silently build the repository default branch.
  2. Build and synth: The pipeline compiles code, runs tests and linting, creates the agent manifest, scans the digest-bound image, validates policies, resolves approved Registry descriptors, and inspects synthesized AWS CloudFormation and cdk-nag output.
  3. Stable roles and permission handoff: The Workload pipeline creates stable Workstream roles and pauses. The Platform pipeline grants exact tool aliases to the exact Gateway role, live policies are verified, and only then does the Workload pipeline continue.
  4. Deploy to nonproduction: The pipeline deploys Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, observability, alarms, budgets, tags, and application resources into the cell’s nonproduction boundary.
  5. Evaluate the deployed agent: The gate invokes the real Runtime and measures regression, quality, tool success, refusal behavior, first-token latency, and cost. Every authorized call is paired with an adversarial twin: the gate calls an approved model and confirms success, then calls an unapproved model and confirms the denial. The same pattern applies to tools, cross-account identity, and throttling. If an expected denial is missing, the gate fails the build.
  6. Human approval: A reviewer examines the deployed evidence, known limitations, and residual risk. A generic green build is not enough when a required probe, resource, or expected denial is missing.
  7. Promote, observe, and roll back: Production promotion uses the reviewed revision and continuity checks. Runtime sessions are sampled through update, cancellation, rollback, restore, and re-run so the pipeline proves both the forward path and recovery path.

No Workstream deployment step has a manual fast track. The Platform team owns the release contract, but Workstream teams operate their own pipeline instances and deployment cadence. Retirement follows a strict dependency order: Platform alias grants are revoked first, then Workstream Gateway and tool roles, then Runtime, Memory, and application resources. Each step is verified before proceeding, and a final inventory confirms zero residual resources remain.

Security and governance

The blueprint implements defense in depth through reinforcing identity, policy, delivery, data, and evidence controls:

  1. Identity and trust boundaries: AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito provide short-lived inference credentials. AWS_IAM and SigV4 authenticate tool traffic. Exact Runtime and Gateway roles, issuer and audience checks, account and Region context, and scoped bootstrap trust limit each principal to its intended path.
  2. Model safety and admission: Inference flows through the governed gateway described in the Solution overview, applying Guardrails and model allow-lists before every call.
  3. Tool authorization: The Tool Gateway invokes only Registry-approved aliases, as detailed in the Solution overview. Cedar policies provide authorization, with a retained AWS Lambda wrapper for defense in depth.
  4. Tenant data protection: Workstream accounts isolate application state. AgentCore memory uses actor-scoped namespaces and customer-managed KMS keys. Tools and application data remain team-owned, and retention, deletion, and access policies are explicit rather than inherited from a shared mutable workload account.
  5. Software supply chain and release: Reviewed source, manifest hashing, reproducible builds, digest-bound image scanning, policy validation, cdk-nag checks, deployed-runtime evaluation, human approval, rollback, and dependency-ordered teardown form one release contract. A missing check fails closed.
  6. Audit, observability, and cost governance: CloudTrail and retained control-plane data corroborate pipeline evidence. OAM shares logs, metrics, and traces with central operators. Standard allocation tags, budgets, quotas, and AWS Cost and Usage Report reconciliation assign ownership without giving the agent permission to rewrite its own attribution.

The repository is a reference implementation. Developers can adjust it to address their needs. The deployment and available features are based on the eu-west-1 (Ireland) Region. A substituted component, another Region, or a wider organizational rollout requires its own availability, security, load, rollback, observability, and teardown evidence.

Conclusion

In this post, we walked through an enterprise Agentic AI Platform built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture separates a centrally governed Platform control plane from repeatable, team-owned Workstream cells, with distinct inference and tool gateways, and production promotion gated by deployed-runtime evaluation.

The companion repository includes a blueprint that validates these controls end to end, from pipeline gates and adversarial boundary tests through zero-residual teardown. The support claim stops at that tested boundary.

To get started, deploy one representative Workstream cell from the companion repository, prove its full lifecycle, and then automate additional cells from the same versioned baseline.

item.title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
item.dc:creator: Sunita Koppar
item.description: The Ray Train Deep Learning Container ships the full CUDA-through-EFA stack, so you build no image. This post walks through a reproducible sample that fine-tunes Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch FSDP across eight GPUs on two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge instances on Amazon EKS, using the container exactly as published.
item.content:encoded:
What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime, a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched.

Figure 1: One EKS cluster with a control plane managed by AWS, a CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) running the KubeRay operator and Ray head, and two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge nodes in one Availability Zone. KubeRay builds it from one RayCluster manifest, Ray Train places eight workers, one per GPU, and inter-node collectives cross over EFA.

Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it.

A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image.

This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository, and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough.

What you get without building anything

The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. The tag this sample pulls, public.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/ray:train-ml-cuda-v1.1, replaces a build that would otherwise look like this:

Layer What you would otherwise build and keep aligned In the Ray Train DLC
Distributed runtime Ray with the dashboard and job server, at a version KubeRay supports Ray 2.58.0 with Train, Tune and Data
Framework PyTorch compiled for your CUDA version PyTorch 2.13.0, torchvision 0.28.0
GPU runtime CUDA, cuDNN and NCCL releases that agree with each other CUDA 13.0.2, cuDNN, NCCL 2.29.7
Networking EFA installer, libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl, built against that NCCL EFA latest, AWS OFI NCCL plugin, GDRCopy
Training libraries DeepSpeed, flash-attn and Transformer Engine compiled for your CUDA DeepSpeed, flash-attn, Transformer Engine, PyTorch Lightning, Hugging Face libraries
Diagnostics NCCL tests built from source all_reduce_perf already on the path

The networking row is the one most teams would least like to own. A mismatch there doesn’t produce an error. NCCL drops to TCP sockets, and the job runs to completion at a fraction of the speed. In the DLC, those libraries are built and tested together, and AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests, which are exactly the paths this sample uses.

A few more properties remove work that you would otherwise do per cluster:

  • No registry setup – The image is public, so nodes pull it without credentials and nothing is built or pushed on the way.
  • No driver matching – On startup the entrypoint checks the host’s NVIDIA driver and, if it is older than the image’s CUDA, turns on the bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries automatically.
  • No head-versus-worker images – The image has no fixed role. Whatever starts the container supplies the ray start command, so one tag serves every pod.
  • No separate inference image family – Ray Train shares the ray ECR repository with the Ray Serve DLC and Ray LLM DLCs, under the train-ml tag prefix.

Configure it, don’t rebuild it

Everything that differs between one training job and the next is set around the image. The sample uses each of these mechanisms:

What you control How you set it In this sample
Head or worker role KubeRay rayStartParams per pod group Same DLC_IMAGE for both. Head runs with num-gpus: "0"
GPUs and EFA per pod Kubernetes resource requests nvidia.com/gpu: 4, vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 1
Network transport Environment variables on the pod or the job FI_PROVIDER, NCCL_NET_PLUGIN, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, NCCL_DEBUG
Extra Python packages Ray runtime_env at submit time Any package a job needs, installed at submit time
Image version Versioned or digest-pinned tag in DLC_IMAGE train-ml-cuda-v1.1
Cluster shape Variables in scripts/env.sh Instance type, node count, GPUs per node, Region, AZ
Training job Arguments to train.py Model, steps, sequence length, batch size

Packages per job. The image ships the HuggingFace training stack, so this sample’s job needs nothing added. When an experiment does need a library the image does not carry, Ray installs it for that job at submit time through runtime_env and the image is unchanged. No new image, no new tag.

Transport per job. The image defaults to FI_PROVIDER=efa, and its NCCL configuration excludes the loopback and Docker bridge interfaces. On EKS you point NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME at the pod’s eth0. The sample sets all four networking variables in the manifest anyway, so the behavior is visible in one file and doesn’t depend on image defaults. Because these are plain environment variables, a single job can override them through its runtime_env.

Versions you choose. The sample pins train-ml-cuda-v1.1, the current minor release, so a cluster is reproducible from one run to the next. The vX.Y tags move with security rebuilds. The fully qualified vX.Y.Z tags stay frozen at the original release build, so pin a digest when you need a byte-identical run. The same image is also available from private ECR URIs.

How the cluster is laid out

Figure 2: The sample’s cluster. Every pod runs the same Ray Train DLC from Amazon ECR Public. The CPU system node runs the KubeRay operator and a Ray head with no GPUs. Each EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge, both in one Availability Zone, runs a single four-GPU Ray worker pod.

All nodes sit in private subnets of one virtual private cloud (VPC) and reach the internet only through a NAT Gateway, which is how every node pulls the DLC from Amazon ECR Public and how workers download model weights from Hugging Face. One m7i.xlarge forms the system node group, hosting kube-system add-ons, the KubeRay operator and the Ray head. The head runs the job server on port 8265 and Ray’s control store on 6379, and it advertises no GPUs, so no training work lands on it. Jobs are submitted from inside the head pod with kubectl exec, through the EKS API, so port 8265 is never exposed outside the cluster.

Training runs on two g6.12xlarge instances, each with four NVIDIA L4 GPUs, 48 vCPUs, 192 GiB of memory, 40 Gbps of networking and one EFA interface. Each runs one Ray worker pod that claims all four GPUs and the EFA interface, and Ray Train places four workers in each pod: ranks 0–3 on one instance, 4–7 on the other. Because EFA traffic doesn’t cross Availability Zones, the scripts place both instances in a single zone that has been checked to offer g6.12xlarge.

What Ray Train does inside the container

The DLC provides the stack. Ray Train provides the part that would otherwise be launcher code. Multi-node PyTorch normally means starting a process per GPU on every host and giving each one its rank, the world size and a rendezvous address. With Ray Train you write the training loop as a function and pass it to TorchTrainer with a ScalingConfig. Ray starts one worker per GPU wherever the cluster has GPUs, forms the torch.distributed process group, and runs your function on each worker.

This sample asks Ray Train for FSDP, which splits the model’s weights, gradients and optimizer state across all eight GPUs rather than copying them to each one. Qwen2.5-1.5B in bfloat16 needs about 12 GB for those four tensors. Sharded eight ways, each L4 GPU holds roughly 1.5 GB. The price is communication: FSDP gathers each layer’s weights before using it and reduce-scatters gradients afterwards, so the whole model crosses between ranks on every step. Between the two instances, that traffic is what the DLC’s EFA stack carries.

Prerequisites

You must have the following in place before you start:

  • Tools: AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 signed in to the target account, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, and envsubst from GNU gettext.
  • Quota: 96 vCPUs of G-family On-Demand capacity for the two g6.12xlarge instances, in an AWS Region where at least one zone offers them. If you already hold an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the instances, set CAPACITY_RESERVATION_ID instead. The scripts launch the node group into it and skip the capacity search.
  • Budget: about $9.50 an hour while the GPU instances are up, covering both instances, the EKS control plane and the NAT Gateway.

A quick way to confirm that the CLI is pointed at the account that you expect:

aws sts get-caller-identity

The training code: One function and a trainer

code/train.py is the whole job, and it contains nothing specific to the container, the cluster or the network. Ray runs train_func once per GPU. It asks Ray for its rank, loads the model, hands it to prepare_model for FSDP, and runs an ordinary PyTorch loop:

code/train.py — the per-GPU function (abridged)

def train_func(config):
    ctx = ray.train.get_context()
    world_size, rank = ctx.get_world_size(), ctx.get_world_rank()
    device = ray.train.torch.get_device()

    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(config["model_id"], torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    # Any submodule above 10M parameters becomes its own FSDP unit. Wrapping by
    # size, not by a model-specific layer class, keeps the script model-agnostic.
    auto_wrap_policy = partial(size_based_auto_wrap_policy, min_num_params=int(1e7))
    model = ray.train.torch.prepare_model(
        model,
        parallel_strategy="fsdp",
        parallel_strategy_kwargs={"auto_wrap_policy": auto_wrap_policy},
    )
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=config["learning_rate"])

    for step in range(config["steps"]):
        input_ids = torch.randint(0, model.config.vocab_size,
            (config["batch_size"], config["seq_len"]), device=device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=input_ids).loss
        loss.backward()  # parameters gathered again, gradients reduce-scattered
        optimizer.step()  # local: each rank updates only its own slice
        ray.train.report({"step": step, "loss": loss.item()})

The driver joins the running cluster, counts its GPUs and starts the trainer. Because the worker count comes from the cluster, the same script runs unchanged on one node or many:

code/train.py — the driver (abridged)

ray.init(address="auto")  # join the RayCluster
num_workers = int(ray.cluster_resources().get("GPU", 0))  # 8 here

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_func,
    train_loop_config={...},
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=num_workers, use_gpu=True),
    run_config=RunConfig(name="ray-train-fsdp-llm"),
)
result = trainer.fit()

The batches are random token IDs so that the run depends on nothing but the cluster. The sample is judged on whether real FSDP collectives crossed both nodes and the job completed. For a real fine-tune, replace the random tensor with a Ray Data or DataLoader pipeline. Nothing else in the function changes.

The manifest: The only place the DLC is configured

manifest/raycluster.yaml is where the image meets the cluster, and it is short because the image needs so little. The head’s only special setting is NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void, which stops the container runtime’s NVIDIA hook from failing on a node that has no GPU. The worker group holds everything else:

manifest/raycluster.yaml — worker group (abridged)

workerGroupSpecs:
  - groupName: gpu-workers
    replicas: 2
    rayStartParams:
      num-gpus: "${GPUS_PER_NODE}"  # keeps Ray's GPU count equal to the pod's
    template:
      spec:
        nodeSelector: { role: gpu-worker }
        containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: "${DLC_IMAGE}"  # the DLC as published; same tag as the head
            env:
              - { name: NCCL_DEBUG, value: "INFO" }  # print the chosen transport
              - { name: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, value: "eth0" }  # pod network on EKS
              - { name: FI_PROVIDER, value: "efa" }  # libfabric: EFA, nothing else
              - { name: NCCL_NET_PLUGIN, value: "ofi" }  # load the AWS OFI plugin
            resources:
              limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: "${GPUS_PER_NODE}", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1",
                cpu: "40", memory: 160Gi }
              requests: { nvidia.com/gpu: "${GPUS_PER_NODE}", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1",
                cpu: "40", memory: 160Gi }

Read it as three decisions.

Which image: ${DLC_IMAGE}, unmodified, for both head and workers.

Which hardware: four GPUs and the node’s single EFA interface per pod. Requesting vpc.amazonaws.com/efa is what makes the EFA device plugin mount the interface into the container. Without it, NCCL can’t see EFA and falls back to sockets.

Which transport: four environment variables, so nothing is left to auto-detection.

Two smaller details keep a multi-node job stable. First, requests should equal limits, which places the workers in Kubernetes’ Guaranteed Quality of Service (QoS) class. This matters because a single throttled or evicted rank stalls the other seven. Second, num-gpus is derived from the same variable as the GPU request, so Ray’s view of capacity always matches Kubernetes’.

Bringing it up: One command for the infrastructure, then the job

Configuration lives in one place, scripts/env.sh: cluster name, Region, Kubernetes version, node types and counts, the image, pinned versions of KubeRay and both device plugins, and the training parameters. Export any of them to change it for a run. All five scripts are idempotent and safe to re-run. deploy_cluster.sh, deploy_node_group.sh, and deploy_ray_train_job.sh each prompt before creating or touching cluster resources. install_gpu_plugins.sh and install_kuberay.sh are reconcilers and run straight through.

cd training/ray-train/scripts
source ./env.sh

./deploy_all.sh – Finds where the capacity actually is, then builds the infrastructure there.

g6.12xlarge capacity shifts between Regions and Availability Zones day to day, so this is the starting point rather than a Region guessed up front in env.sh. It first runs find_gpu_capacity.sh, which checks, per candidate Region: whether g6.12xlarge is offered in each Availability Zone, whether the account’s On-Demand G/VT-family vCPU quota has room for the requested node count, and the EC2 Spot placement score as a capacity signal. With --probe, which deploy_all.sh passes by default, it gets a definitive answer by creating and immediately canceling a real Capacity Reservation in each candidate zone. It then shows the plan and asks once:

Proceed with the whole chain without further prompts? (y/N):

Answering y runs, in order, deploy_cluster.sh, deploy_node_group.sh, install_gpu_plugins.sh, and install_kuberay.sh in the recommended Region, each skipping its own repeat confirmation because this one already asked (-y skips this prompt too, and --plan shows the plan without creating anything). If the GPU node group can’t launch in the best zone, the script removes it and tries the next zone the probe confirmed. GPU_AZ is also cross-checked against the cluster’s actual private subnets, not only where g6.12xlarge happens to be offered, so the GPU node group can’t end up pinned to an Availability Zone the cluster has no subnet in. The chosen Region and zone are saved to scripts/.placement.env, which every other script reads, so later commands target the same place without re-exporting anything. Together the four steps take 20 to 30 minutes on a fresh Region. An existing cluster or node group is detected and reused.

deploy_cluster.sh creates the EKS control plane, VPC, OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, core add-ons, and the m7i.xlarge system node group, choosing subnets in zones that actually offer g6.12xlarge. deploy_node_group.sh adds the two g6.12xlarge instances with EFA turned on, labeled role=gpu-worker and nvidia.com/gpu.present=true. The second label is one that teams often overlook. Without it, the NVIDIA device plugin chart’s DaemonSet runs on zero nodes, with no error pointing at the cause. install_gpu_plugins.sh makes sure both device plugins are present. Recent eksctl bundles them into an EFA-enabled node group, so on a fresh cluster it finds them and skips. Otherwise it installs them at pinned chart versions. Either way it verifies nvidia.com/gpu and vpc.amazonaws.com/efa are allocatable on every GPU node rather than trusting a successful Helm release. install_kuberay.sh installs the KubeRay operator onto the system node, keeping it off the GPU instances.

What deploy_all.sh does not do by default is run the training job. That stays a separate step you can re-run as often as you like, because it is a real job run rather than infrastructure, and a failed job then never sends you back through cluster setup. Pass --train to chain it:

./deploy_ray_train_job.sh — the RayCluster, the job, and the checks.

Renders the manifest with envsubst and applies it. It then re-reads each GPU node’s allocatable resources before waiting on any pod: if a device plugin didn’t come up, you get a clear error here rather than a pod that sits in Pending until a timeout. Once the head is Ready and both workers are Ready, it copies code/ onto the head and, through kubectl exec, submits from inside it:

ray job submit --address http://localhost:8265 --working-dir /tmp/ray-train-code \
python3 train.py --model_id Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B

The submit call streams logs from all eight ranks and returns when the job does. The script then inspects which transport NCCL used and exits with an error if the job failed or EFA wasn’t in the path, which also makes it usable as a continuous integration (CI) gate. ./deploy_ray_train_job.sh status prints the RayCluster state, which instance hosts each pod, and GPU capacity. A correctly provisioned cluster looks like this:

$ kubectl get nodes -l role=gpu-worker \
-o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,GPU:.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu,EFA:.status.allocatable.vpc\.amazonaws\.com/efa'
NAME               GPU   EFA
ip-192-168-70-51   4     1
ip-192-168-92-26   4     1

Figure 3: One FSDP step on this cluster. Weights are gathered in the forward and backward passes and gradients are reduce-scattered. Traffic between the instances takes the path the DLC ships, NCCL → AWS OFI NCCL plugin → libfabric → EFA, or falls back to TCP sockets when that path is missing.

Adapting it to your workload

Because the image is used as published and the job learns its scale from the cluster, most changes touch exactly one file:

You want to change Where No changes needed to
The model MODEL_ID Code, manifest, image
Steps, sequence length, batch size STEPS, SEQ_LEN, BATCH_SIZE Code, manifest, image
The training loop itself Body of train_func Trainer, manifest, image, scripts
An additional Python package --runtime-env-json pip list Image
A pinned DLC release DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag Everything else
The GPU instance family GPU_NODE_TYPE, GPUS_PER_NODE Code, image
How many GPU instances GPU_NODE_COUNT, plus replicas, minReplicas and maxReplicas in the manifest Code (it counts the GPUs)
Region or zone REGION, optionally GPU_AZ Everything else

Variables in the table live in env.sh unless stated otherwise. When switching instance families, GPUS_PER_NODE has to match the hardware, and the family needs EFA support plus a place on the EFA device plugin’s list of allowed instance types. The plugin version pinned here is known to include g6.12xlarge. Moving to p5 or another GPUDirect-capable family needs no change to the image or the training code.

Tearing it down

The GPU instances are the expensive part, at around $9.50 an hour together with the control plane and NAT Gateway. Remove things in the opposite order to how they were created:

./delete_ray_train_job.sh        # RayCluster
./install_kuberay.sh cleanup     # KubeRay operator
./install_gpu_plugins.sh cleanup # NVIDIA and EFA device plugins
./delete_node_group.sh           # GPU instances
./delete_cluster.sh              # EKS cluster, VPC and system node

Where to go next

Two instances and eight GPUs ran a sharded fine-tune on EKS with a container nobody built. The Ray Train DLC supplied a tested stack from CUDA through EFA. KubeRay started it as head and workers from one tag. Ray Train placed the workers and formed the process group. Everything that varied, from hardware to transport to Python packages, was set from outside the image. The EFA path the image ships engaged with four environment variables and doubled throughput over TCP on unchanged code.

Natural next moves:

  • Replace the random batches with a real dataset, and checkpoint to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon FSx for Lustre.
  • Pin DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag for reproducible runs.
  • Turn on FailureConfig so long runs survive a lost instance.
  • Move to a larger model on a GPUDirect RDMA family such as p5. The image and code stay the same.

item.title: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3
item.dc:creator: Vinicius Pedroni
item.description: As QA test automation spreads across an organization, organizing tests and controlling who owns them becomes the real work. Part 3 of the QA Studio series on Amazon Nova Act adds applications that organize tests and report health metrics, plus team-based user management that controls who can see and change what.
item.content:encoded:
As quality assurance (QA) automation adoption grows inside an organization, a new problem appears that has nothing to do with writing tests. A platform team stands up test automation, then a second team wants to join, then a dozen more. Soon hundreds of test cases belong to different products and squads, and everyone can see everyone else’s tests. No one can answer a basic question at a glance: is this application’s test coverage healthy right now? Test authoring stops being the bottleneck. Organizing tests and controlling who can touch them becomes the work.

A second, related question follows close behind: who owns this application and its tests, and who is accountable when coverage slips? Without a clear owner, health problems have no one to land on.

In the first post, we introduced QA Studio, a reference solution built with Amazon Nova Act. Teams use it to define tests in natural language and run them through AI-powered visual navigation. In the second post, we added test suites and a CLI for batch regression testing in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. In this post, we cover two capabilities that help QA Studio scale across an organization. The first, applications, organizes tests and reports health metrics. The second, team-based user management, controls who can see and change what.

Organizing tests with applications

An application in QA Studio represents the system under test: a website, a web app, a service front end. It’s the container that gives a collection of tests, a home, and an owner. Use cases (the individual tests from Part 1) and test suites (the regression collections from Part 2) belong to an application, and they inherit its ownership. Instead of one flat list of every test in the deployment, each team works inside the applications they own.

Creating an application takes a name, a base URL, and an optional set of environments such as development, staging, and production. From the application page, teams create new use cases directly in context, add existing ones, and group them into test suites. This is also where QA Studio reports on the health of the tests it runs.

Figure 1: The application detail page, showing pass rate, executions, and failures with the use cases and test suites tabs

Understanding application health with metrics

Tests produce results. Understanding those results over time is what tells a team whether the development lifecycle for an application is healthy, not only whether a single build is ready for release. QA Studio records the outcome of every execution as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by application and by environment. It turns these metrics into a health view on the application page.

The top of the page answers the immediate question with three figures: the pass rate over the selected window, the total number of executions, and the current failure count. Alongside them, QA Studio computes a health score of 0–100. The score starts from the pass rate and subtracts a penalty for flaky tests. That way, an application whose tests pass but flip between pass and fail doesn’t present a falsely perfect picture. A team scanning a portfolio of applications can tell the stable ones from the ones that need attention without opening each result.

The metrics tab moves from the current snapshot to trends. Teams choose a 7-day window with hourly granularity or a 30-day window with daily granularity, and QA Studio charts executions, successes, failures, and average duration across that period. Because the underlying metrics carry an environment dimension, teams filter the view to a single environment. For example, they can compare how staging behaves against production for the same set of tests.

Two views target the tests that cost teams the most time. The flaky tests view ranks use cases by how often they flipped between passing and failing over the last seven days. This surfaces the intermittent failures that erode trust in a suite before they turn into a production miss. The recent failures view lists the latest failed executions for quick triage. Each one links back to the Amazon Nova Act trajectory logs and session recordings described in Part 1. That way, moving from “this test is failing” to “here is exactly what the agent saw” takes one click.

Figure 2: The metrics tab: pass rate, executions, and average duration over the selected window, with the daily success-and-failure chart, failure hotspots, and the flaky use case ranking

Controlling access with teams and roles

Metrics tell a team how their applications are doing. Team-based user management decides which applications are theirs in the first place. QA Studio organizes access around teams, and an application belongs to exactly one team. Members of that team work with its applications. Everyone else doesn’t see them.

Every team member holds one of five roles, and each role includes the permissions of the ones below it:

  • Admin: Studio-wide access to every team, application, and user, including creating teams and assigning applications. Admin is a studio-wide role rather than a per-team assignment.
  • Team Lead: Manages their own team members and creates applications for the team.
  • Editor: Creates and edits use cases and test suites within the team’s applications.
  • Executor: Runs use cases and suites but doesn’t modify them.
  • Viewer: Read-only access to the team’s applications and results.

Because roles are cumulative, a Team Lead has everything an Editor has, and so on down to Viewer. Access to a use case or a test suite follows the application that contains it. If a member can work with the application, they can work with its tests, bounded by their role. This keeps permission management at the application level instead of on thousands of individual tests.

An administrator sees the whole studio. The Users page lists every account with its team and role in one place. An admin can tell who holds Team Lead on which team and who carries Studio-wide Administrator rights. In the reference deployment shown here, four users span two teams: two Team Leads, one Viewer, and one Studio-wide Administrator. The Teams page rolls the same data up by team, showing each team’s member count and application count side by side. An admin can see which teams are expanding before opening any one of them.

Figure 3: The studio-wide Users page: every account with its team and role, filterable by team and by role

The same membership data, rolled up by team, appears on the Teams page.

Figure 4: The Teams page: each team with its member and application counts

Switching from teams to applications, the studio-wide Applications list shows every application across all teams.

Figure 5: The studio-wide Applications list: every application with its base URL, owning team, use-case count, and last execution status

Sharing applications between teams

Teams rarely work in complete isolation. A platform team might own an application that a feature team needs to run against, without handing over the ability to change it. QA Studio supports this with shared access: the owning team grants another team access to an application at a view, execute, or full level.

Shared access follows a ceiling rule. A user’s effective permission on a shared application is the lower of their own role and the level of the grant. A Viewer who is given full access to a shared application remains view-only, because their role is the ceiling. This way, an owning team can share widely without granting more than a recipient’s role allows.

What a team lead sees

A team lead works inside a single team rather than the whole studio. Opening My Team presents four tabs that cover everything the lead controls: Members, Applications, Use Cases, and Shared Access. The Members tab lists the people on the team. The lead can change any member’s role inline or add a new one, so day-to-day access management stays with the person closest to the work. In the AWS Team shown here, the lead manages two members, one Team Lead and one Viewer.

Figure 6: The team lead’s Members tab, with inline role assignment for each member

The Applications tab shows only the applications the team owns, each with its test-case count and last-run time. This keeps the lead focused on their own surface rather than the full studio inventory. The Shared Access tab is where cross-team sharing becomes concrete. Here the AWS Team has granted the AMZN Team view access to an application, and the lead can grant, revoke, or change the level of that access. Because the grant was view level, an AMZN Team Editor still sees the shared application read-only: the ceiling rule from the previous section, applied in practice.

Figure 7: The team lead’s Applications tab, scoped to the team’s own applications

The same Team Lead’s Shared Access tab records which other teams can reach the team’s applications, and at what level.

Figure 8: The team lead’s Shared Access tab, showing a view-level grant to another team

How it works

QA Studio builds team-based access control and metrics on the same serverless foundation described in the earlier posts, adding a few AWS services to the mix:

  • Amazon Cognito: Each team maps to a set of Cognito groups, one per role. An AWS Lambda authorizer resolves a caller’s groups into API scopes and team context on every request.
  • Amazon DynamoDB: Teams, memberships, application ownership, and cross-team share grants are stored in the existing single-table design.
  • Amazon CloudWatch: Every execution emits custom metrics in the QAStudio/Executions namespace, dimensioned by application and environment. The metrics API reads them back to build the health view and trend charts.
  • AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway: The backend enforces access at two layers: the scope a caller’s role grants, and a resource check that confirms the caller’s team owns or has been shared with the application.

Because access is derived from Cognito group membership, the OAuth client credentials flow from Part 2 fits the same model. A CI pipeline authenticates as a machine identity with the scopes it needs and no more.

Getting started

Applications, metrics, and team-based access control are part of the QA Studio reference solution, which you deploy in your own AWS account with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). All test data, results, and metrics stay within your account boundaries. After deploying, an administrator creates teams, assigns members and roles, and assigns applications to teams. Each team’s health metrics begin populating as their tests run.

For deployment instructions and configuration details, see the QA Studio GitHub repository and its documentation.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how QA Studio scales agentic QA automation from individual tests to an organization. Applications give every team a home for their use cases and test suites. They report health through pass rate, trend charts, a flaky-adjusted health score, and failure triage built on Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Team-based user management, backed by Amazon Cognito, keeps each team working within the applications they own, with cross-team sharing bounded by a clear ceiling rule.

These capabilities build on the natural language test authoring from Part 1 and the suites and CI/CD integration from Part 2. Together, they help QA automation grow across many teams without losing visibility or control. To try it in your own environment, deploy the reference solution from the QA Studio GitHub repository, create your first team and application, and run a few use cases to watch the metrics take shape. To learn more about the agent behind it, see the Amazon Nova Act product page.

 

About the authors

Vinicius Pedroni

Vinicius is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS for the Travel and Hospitality Industry, with focus on Edge Services and Generative AI. Vinicius is also passionate about assisting customers on their Cloud Journey, allowing them to adopt the right strategies at the right moment.

Jan Wiemers

Jan is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, working with customers in the Travel, Transportation & Logistics industry. With over 20 years of experience in the software industry, he focuses on the AI Product Development Lifecycle and Test Automation, helping customers accelerate how they build, test, and deploy AI-driven solutions.

item.title: AWS named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service
item.dc:creator: Pasquale DeMaio
item.description: AWS has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for AWS Connect Customer. This recognition marks an important milestone for our team, and it reflects years of work pushing on what's possible in customer experience.
item.content:encoded:
I’m proud to share that Amazon Web Services (AWS) has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for Amazon Connect for the fourth consecutive year. We believe this recognition reflects years of work pushing on what’s possible in customer experience.

When we launched Amazon Connect Customer, we set out to evolve how businesses serve their customers: to make personalized, intelligent experiences possible without giving up efficiency, flexibility, or control. That belief still drives how we build today.

Customer expectations have shifted. People expect you to recognize them, understand what they need, and stay consistent across every channel. They don’t want to repeat themselves. They don’t want to navigate disconnected systems to solve a simple problem. They want interactions that feel natural, relevant, and genuinely helpful. Meeting that takes more than traditional contact center technology, it takes a comprehensive solution that brings together customer context, AI, and the flexibility to adapt. That’s what we’re building with Amazon Connect Customer.

Customer experience without compromise

What matters most to your customers hasn’t changed: they want to be known, they want their problems fully resolved, and they want to trust you in the moments that matter. Read the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant to know why we are recognized.

Experiences that start with knowing the customer.  Connect Customer builds a living picture of every customer: who they are, what they’ve been through, what they need next. Every touchpoint draws on that intelligence. Your customer feels known before a single word is exchanged. That’s what personal actually looks like.

Resolution that carries all the way through.

Most of the industry is still optimizing for deflection: getting customers away from humans as fast as possible. We took a different path. Connect Customer is built for the hard things: the disputed claim, the renegotiated mortgage, the disrupted itinerary that needs real action and can’t go wrong. We carry those interactions all the way through to resolution, and we make them feel natural and personal.

Generative and agentic AI push this further: understanding what a customer needs and acting on it. Every action is auditable. Humans step in when the moment calls for it. You get enterprise scale and the confidence that nothing slips through the cracks.

Building for what’s next

The companies that win the next decade of customer experience won’t be the ones with the most channels or the fastest bot. They’ll be the ones whose customers feel known, whose problems actually get resolved, and whose trust is earned in the moments that matter most. Connect Customer exists to make that real for businesses of every size.

I’m proud of the Connect Customer team for receiving this recognition for the fourth year in a row. Our engineers, product teams, partners, and customers shaped what we’ve built. This is a moment to celebrate how far we’ve come, and a signal of what’s ahead.

Every customer is unique. Every interaction should reflect that.
