item.title: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
item.dc:creator: Kanwaljit Khurmi
item.description: Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs takes full container image download off the critical path. SageMaker AI lazy-loads your image to start containers in seconds instead of minutes, with no changes to your job definition. See the benchmarks and how to adopt it.
item.content:encoded:
Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs, which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job.

With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure.

SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks.

This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs.

The challenge

SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk.

For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime.

How SOCI indexing works

Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it.

A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid.

SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically

When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly:

Scenario What happens
The image includes a SOCI index SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes
The image has no SOCI index Standard download, no change in behavior
The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed The job falls back to a standard download and continues running

Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow.

What we measured

We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed.

Setup

  • Eight images, 1.8–35.4 GB compressed.
  • GPU and CPU instances ml.g4dn, ml.g5, ml.g6, ml.g6e, ml.g7, ml.g7e, ml.p4d, ml.p5, and ml.m7i, from xlarge to 48xlarge, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) and the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1).
  • Download time measured from the start of the image pull until the container is ready to run. All figures are medians of repeated runs.

Result 1: Download time drops from minutes to seconds at every image size

Image size (compressed) Standard download Lazy loading Improvement
1.8 GB 48 s 3-11 s ~8x
13.2 GB 3 min 42 s ~6 s ~34x
35.4 GB 7 min 17 s 3-11 s ~38x

The following chart compares container image download time for a standard Docker pull against SOCI lazy loading across eight image sizes, from 1.8 GB to 35.4 GB.

Each image size shows two bars. The Docker download time bar (blue) grows steadily with image size, from 48 seconds at 1.8 GB to 7 minutes 17 seconds at 35.4 GB.

A speedup label above each pair shows the ratio of Docker time to SOCI time. Speedups range from approximately 10x for the smallest image to over 35x for the largest.

Figure 1: Container image download time, standard Docker pull compared to SOCI lazy loading, across eight image sizes

Standard download time grows with image size because every file is decompressed and written. Lazy loading stayed at 3–11 seconds regardless of size, an 8x–46x improvement. The bigger the image, the more minutes you save.

Result 2: The saving holds on every instance type and size

Running the 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type/size combinations, standard download ranged from 3 min 16 s to 4 min 20 s, while lazy loading held at 6-8 s. That is about 34x faster on every configuration. You don’t need to change instance type or size to benefit.

Figure 2: Download time for a 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type and size combinations

Result 3: Training performance is unaffected beyond a first-epoch penalty

We ran two kinds of full training jobs from the Docker-pulled and from the SOCI-indexed image and compared every epoch:

  • Image classification on ResNet-50 on Imagenette (9,469 images)
    • Container images: PyTorch (13.2 GB DLC) and TensorFlow (9.9 GB DLC)
    • Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g7e.48xlarge, ml.g7.48xlarge, ml.g6e.12xlarge, ml.g6e.24xlarge, and ml.g6e.48xlarge.
  • Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning: full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Qwen2.5-0.5B on alpaca-cleaned (51,760 examples) with the Hugging Face Trainer.
    • Container image: 9.4 GB Hugging Face PyTorch DLC.
    • Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g6.48xlarge.

The following chart breaks job startup into image download time and first training epoch time, comparing a standard Docker pull with a SOCI-indexed image across GPU and CPU configurations for both workloads.

Figure 3: Job startup split into image download time and first training epoch time, standard Docker pull compared to a SOCI-indexed image

  • From the second epoch on, time per epoch is the same (within run-to-run variation) on every instance, for both workloads.
  • The first epoch takes 3–16 s longer from the lazy-loaded image, while files the framework touches for the first time are fetched. This first-epoch cost is the same on every instance size.
  • Net: each job finished 1-6 min sooner. That is the download saving minus the one-time first-epoch cost, a fixed saving per job.

Test this on your own workload

These numbers are from the two workloads described earlier. The first-epoch cost depends on your image and what your code touches at startup:

  • Lazy loading wins when the first training step needs only a fraction of the image, the rest streams in while you train.
  • If your entry point reads most of the image before training starts (for example, scanning, checksumming, or preloading its contents), the first epoch waits for roughly the same bytes a full pull would have fetched. The net improvement would be small.
  • Front-loaded starts still came out ahead in our tests:
    • torch.compile and a just-in-time (JIT) built CUDA extension added 7-15 s to the first epoch (net saving still 3 min 25 s–3 min 56 s)
    • A 6 GB model baked into the image streamed its weights at load time, adding 2-3.5 min, but the overall job still finished 2-2.5 mins sooner on the indexed image.

Getting started

You can adopt SOCI indexing two ways: use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container or create an index for your own custom image.

Option 1: Use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container

AWS publishes SOCI-indexed variants of several popular Deep Learning Containers, identified by the -soci suffix on the image tag:

763104351884.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/pytorch-training:2.9-gpu-py312-cu130-ubuntu22.04-sagemaker-v1-soci

Pre-indexed variants are available for PyTorch Training, TensorFlow Training, vLLM, and SGLang, including arm64 variants for some frameworks. To adopt lazy loading, update the image tag in your job definition to the -soci variant. Browse the full list in the AWS Deep Learning Containers Gallery.

Note: If you build your own image FROM a DLC base image, you must create a SOCI index for your final image. The index from the base image does not carry forward to derived images.

Option 2: Create a SOCI index for your own image

To index a custom image, you need a Linux host (such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance running Amazon Linux 2023) with containerd, the SOCI snapshotter, and either Finch or nerdctl installed.

  1. Set your environment variables. 
    ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333"
REGION="us-east-1"
REPOSITORY_NAME="my-training-image"
ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG="v1.0"
SOCI_IMAGE_TAG="v1.0-soci"
REGISTRY="$ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com"
  2. Install the required tools. 
    sudo dnf install -y containerd fuse soci-snapshotter runfinch-finch
sudo systemctl start soci-snapshotter
sudo systemctl restart containerd
  3. Authenticate to Amazon ECR. 
    aws ecr get-login-password --region "$REGION" \
  | sudo nerdctl login -u AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"
  4. Pull your original image. 
    sudo nerdctl pull "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG"
  5. Create the SOCI-indexed image. 
    sudo nerdctl image convert --soci \
  "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG" \
  "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG"
  6. Push the indexed image. 
    sudo nerdctl push --platform linux/amd64 \
  "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG"

This creates two artifacts in your repository: the SOCI index and an OCI-compliant image index manifest linking your image to the index. Your original image and its digest remain unchanged.

Automate index creation in CI/CD

To generate indexes automatically on every push, deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder. It uses an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect Amazon ECR image push events and build the index. No changes to your build pipeline are required.

Use the indexed image in your SageMaker AI job

Reference your SOCI-indexed image exactly as you would any other image. No API changes are needed. Only the tag differs.

Training example (SageMaker Python SDK)

from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer
from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute

trainer = ModelTrainer(
    training_image="111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-training-image:v1.0-soci",
    role="arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/SageMakerExecutionRole",
    compute=Compute(
        instance_type="ml.g5.12xlarge",
        instance_count=2,
    ),
)

trainer.train()

Verify that your image includes a SOCI index

Before launching, confirm your tag resolves to an indexed image:

aws ecr batch-get-image \
  --repository-name "$REPOSITORY_NAME" \
  --image-ids imageTag="$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" \
  --accepted-media-types \
  "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
  --query 'images[0].imageManifest' --output text \
  | jq '.manifests[] | {mediaType, artifactType}'

Look for a child manifest whose artifactType begins with application/vnd.amazon.soci.index. alongside your platform manifest. If it isn’t there, the tag does not point to an indexed image.

Things to keep in mind

  • Amazon ECR private repositories only. Images in other registries, or pulled through a private Docker registry (TrainingRepositoryAccessMode set to Vpc), are not eligible for lazy loading.
  • Improvement scales with image size. Images smaller than roughly 4 GB see relatively small improvements.
  • Check for Docker-specific assumptions. SOCI-indexed images run on a containerd-based runtime. Review entry points and setup scripts for code that calls the Docker CLI, reads /var/run/docker.sock, or derives identifiers from cgroup paths. SageMaker AI mounts a /.dockerenv marker for backward compatibility, but avoid adding new dependencies on it.
  • SOCI indexing for SageMaker AI jobs is available across all AWS Regions.

Conclusion

With SOCI indexing, you can minimize container image download time from your SageMaker AI training and processing jobs. Add a SOCI index to your images, or switch to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container. Either way, you cut startup time from minutes to seconds, reduce total job cost, and accelerate your machine learning (ML) iteration cycle. And your existing job definitions, API calls, and data pipelines stay exactly the same.

To learn more about Amazon SageMaker AI and start using SOCI indexing, explore the following resources:

  1. Pick a SOCI-indexed Deep Learning Container. Browse the Deep Learning Containers Gallery and append -soci to your image tag. For framework-specific guidance, see SOCI index for AWS Deep Learning Containers.
  2. Index your own custom image. Follow the step-by-step walkthrough in the SageMaker AI Developer Guide, or refer to the SOCI snapshotter getting-started guide for advanced options.
  3. Automate indexing in your CI/CD pipeline. Deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder to generate indexes automatically on every image push. No pipeline changes are required.
  4. Test locally with Finch. Use the Finch lazy-loading walkthrough to validate your image on a containerd-based runtime before you submit a job.
  5. Dive deeper into the technology. item.title: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock
item.dc:creator: Khaled Thabit
item.description: Property Finder found that 96.8% of their vision-AI evaluation labels were inherited from the incumbent model, hiding its true accuracy. See how they built unbiased ground truth, applied evolutionary prompt optimization, and selected a more accurate, cost-effective model on Amazon Bedrock, cutting cost by 86% across 11 image-quality attributes.
item.content:encoded:
This post was co-authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder.

The engineering team at Property Finder, a digital real estate application, discovered that 96.8 percent of their evaluation labels had been inherited directly from a single model’s predictions rather than verified by human experts. Their ground truth was systematically skewed toward the incumbent model, making every alternative appear to underperform. The labels also had errors, but the bias was what blocked objective model comparison. They uncovered this when migrating their vision AI workload to a more cost-effective option on Amazon Bedrock.

Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images every day across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Their system evaluates 11 quality attributes per image. These cover watermark detection, room classification, furnishing status, photo quality, and construction indicators. That’s thousands of new property listings with an average of 15 images each. All need quality assessment before going live.

Property Finder needed a more cost-effective option. But measured against those labels, any alternative was at a disadvantage.

The hardest part was not finding a better model. It was discovering that their evaluation methodology itself was the blocker.

In this post, we share how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to select the right model on Amazon Bedrock, achieving higher accuracy at 86 percent lower cost. We walk through the methodology and iteration examples, with lessons you can apply to your own workloads.

The following figure illustrates the prompt optimization loop that Property Finder and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team used to iteratively improve classification accuracy on Amazon Bedrock.

Figure 1: Prompt optimization loop architecture

The diagram shows the iterative prompt optimization cycle. A property image is processed by Amazon Bedrock, which outputs the predicted attributes in JSON format. During optimization, these predictions are scored with Micro F1 against the 256-image expert-annotated development set. Error analysis then inspects failed images and identifies visual patterns, which inform the next prompt version. The loop ran from v0 to v27. AI assistants helped refine the prompts, and later versions used automated optimization.

Your evaluation might be lying

Many teams encounter this scenario. You want to compare vision models, so you build an evaluation dataset. The most common way to get labels is to run your current model and treat its outputs as ground truth. The model has been running in production and nobody complained, so the labels must be good enough.

But this creates a circular evaluation where any alternative gets judged by how closely it matches the incumbent’s behavior, not by actual correctness.

Property Finder’s evaluation dataset had exactly this problem. Of their labeled samples, 96.8 percent came directly from the predictions of the existing vision language model (VLM) rather than independent human verification. Any alternative model was structurally disadvantaged before a single image was even processed.

Hidden errors confirmed the severity. Watermark text extraction had character-level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters. Photo classification forced single labels onto images containing multiple room types.

In the remaining 3.2 percent of human-labeled samples, annotators had introduced categories outside the original specification, like Office appearing where no such label existed in the prompt. A model comparison loses validity when the answer key was written by the model you are trying to replace.

Building ground truth you can trust

To break the cycle, you need human experts with real domain knowledge doing fresh annotations independently. No reference to previous model outputs. No access to what the incumbent predicted.

Dataset scope

Property Finder’s team hand-annotated 356 UAE images and a separate set of Egypt images. The team selected these from unlabeled production listings across representative industry segments. This post reports results on the UAE images. The Egypt images served as a cross-regional check on 230 images and are not reported here. The first 256 UAE images to be annotated formed the development set for tuning. The evaluation set for the final model comparison uses all 356, adding 100 images annotated after the development runs. A set of 356 images is roughly sufficient to detect moderate differences between models. Rare classes within individual attributes have fewer examples, so smaller differences on those attributes might not be detectable.

Expert annotation

A strategy and analytics expert annotated all images. They brought specialized knowledge of real estate listing quality standards. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team conducted systematic quality reviews through dedicated clarification sessions. Those reviews settled ambiguous cases and kept the labeling consistent across the dataset.

Multi-label transition

Real estate images frequently show multiple rooms through doorways or display overlapping quality characteristics. The switch from single-label to multi-label classification alleviated a major source of artificial ambiguity.

A hallway photo showing a bedroom through a doorway is genuinely both. After you allow multiple labels, you measure what the model gets right rather than penalizing it for reasonable secondary predictions.

A hybrid approach could complement this methodology: models from different families surface candidate labels and disagreements, and human experts adjudicate every case, so no model output is used directly as a label. This would reduce the annotation burden for future dataset expansion.

Metrics selection

Micro F1 served as the primary metric because it weights each prediction equally, which matches the business goal of overall label correctness. Macro F1 was reported alongside it because Micro F1 is dominated by frequent classes and can hide weak performance on rare attributes. Per-label precision and recall helped identify specific failure modes. Per-sample intersection over union (IoU) measured how closely each image’s predicted labels overlapped the expert’s labels. The nine single-label attributes, such as rotation or watermark detection, have one right answer per image. The AWS team also scored them with exact-match accuracy, the share of images where the answer matches the expert label.

Prompt optimization as reinforcement learning

With unbiased evaluation in place, you can start improving. You cannot improve what you cannot measure correctly.

The optimization follows a loop analogous to reinforcement learning. Think of each prompt version as an agent, the Micro F1 score as the reward signal, and error analysis as the gradient for improvement. The idea resembles GEPA (Genetic-Pareto reflective prompt evolution), where you mutate prompt components, evaluate fitness, select survivors, and iterate. In this engagement, the AWS team refined most versions from error analysis, with AI assistants reviewing failed images and proposing changes.

MIPROv2, an automated prompt optimization framework from the DSPy library, complemented this manual process for the photo classification task in v27.

Where it started

The first prompt (v0) used generic classification instructions, simplified here for illustration:

“Classify this image into one of the following categories: Living Room, Kitchen, Bedroom, Bathroom…”

Proprietary model A, Property Finder’s production baseline, scored a Micro F1 of 0.55 on the 256-image development set. It used v22, a prompt tuned for its model family. Scores before v21 used the earlier single-label setup and aren’t directly comparable.

Iteration by iteration

The AWS team tested early versions on several candidate models and added structured output formatting and attribute-specific definitions.

The most instructive fix came from image-level error analysis. In the early single-label versions, the model consistently classified rooms visible through doorways as the secondary room type. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team added explicit instructions to classify based on the room occupying the majority of the frame. The later switch to multi-label output kept the main room as a label and allowed rooms visible through doorways as additional labels.

Regional customization produced the next gain. In some regions, listing photos carry decorative Arabic text overlays that are not watermarks. Rules for that text removed a whole category of false positives.

The v21 prompt switched photo classification and room category to multi-label output and became the shared starting prompt for every model. With it, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct from Meta scored a Micro F1 of 0.75 on the development set. From there, the AWS team tuned each model’s prompt separately. For this model, v24 targeted room size overestimation, multi-label handling, and output format. Then v25, an automatically optimized version, moved the critical tasks first. In v27, MIPROv2 restructured the photo classification task, and the model’s Micro F1 on that task reached 0.76.

Where it ended

The final prompt, v27_PF, is v27 plus rules that Property Finder added for renders, images with borders or frames, and corridors. Like v27, it keeps the Arabic text rules and output format instructions. A normalization step after each model call handles remaining format differences.

With v27_PF, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct scored a Micro F1 of 0.80 on the 356-image evaluation set, where proprietary model A scored 0.56 with v22. The evaluation set includes the 256 development images, and both models’ prompts were tuned on those images. These scores are therefore optimistic.

The switch from proprietary model A to Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, each on its own tuned prompt, lifted Micro F1 from 0.55 to 0.81 on the development set. That is a 47 percent relative gain. Prompt tuning alone, on Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, raised it from 0.75 with the shared v21 prompt to 0.81 with v27.

Lessons from failed approaches

Not everything succeeded. The 2-bucket approach put the watermark attributes and the other attributes in two separate API calls. It brought no meaningful accuracy gain. Boxed-image detection also dropped sharply. Without the watermark attributes in the same prompt, the models mistook watermark overlays for image borders.

Generic prompts also failed regardless of which model you ran them on. Real estate imagery has too much domain specificity for a one-size-fits-all instruction.

Results: Cost, accuracy, and speed

The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team evaluated multiple models on Amazon Bedrock with the unbiased evaluation framework. All models started from the shared v21 prompt and were then tuned for their model family on the development set. Proprietary model A got one tuning round, v22. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct got several, v24 to v27, plus Property Finder’s edge-case rules, so it had more tuning effort behind it. The final comparison against proprietary model A used the 356-image evaluation set. Property Finder selected Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct for their production workload based on accuracy across all 11 attributes and cost efficiency. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

The following table shows the exact-match accuracy that Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct (v27_PF) reached on each single-label attribute, scored on the 356-image evaluation set. It scored 90 percent or higher on six of the nine, and matched or exceeded proprietary model A on all 11 attributes. On photo classification, which can have several labels per image, the two scored the same.

Attribute Exact-match accuracy
Rotation detection 100%
People detection 97%
Boxed-image detection 97%
Watermark detection 94%
Render detection 93%
Furnished status 91%
Room under construction 81%
Room size 65%
Watermark text extraction 55%

Cost per 1,000 images

Property Finder scores tens of thousands of images a day, so per-image cost matters. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct is a cost-effective open-weight model, and the pipeline gets all attributes for an image in a single call.

Result Value
Estimated cost per 1,000 images $2.35
Cost reduction compared with Property Finder’s previous setup 86%

These figures are estimates as of December 2025 in the US East (Ohio) Region. The Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct figure assumes 9,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens per image, from the original two-call cost analysis. A single call with the production prompt carries about 7,500–8,000 input tokens, so this is an upper estimate. The 86 percent compares it with the cost analysis estimate for Property Finder’s previous setup, which used the v21 prompt. The accuracy comparison used v22, which was tuned from v21, so its cost might differ. For current pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Inference speed

Property Finder runs this optimized pipeline in production, processing tens of thousands of images daily with Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct on Amazon Bedrock. In their own monitoring, Property Finder observed a 40–60 percent reduction in inference latency compared with their previous setup.

Apply this to your workloads

Start by auditing your evaluation labels. If they came from model predictions rather than human experts, you have the same bias problem Property Finder found.

Build domain-expert ground truth for a few hundred representative samples, and keep a separate test split that you never use for tuning. Adopt multi-label metrics where your classification task involves overlapping attributes. Then iterate on prompts using image error analysis, treating each iteration as a generation in an evolutionary optimization loop.

When you deploy a pipeline like this, add responsible AI controls. For example, you can use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content policies and filter inappropriate model outputs. The attribute predictions in this pipeline don’t come with a calibrated confidence score, so use a practical signal to choose images for human review. Model disagreement is one such signal. When two models give different answers for an attribute, the image is often ambiguous. A second model on every image adds cost, so you can start with a sample. Check how often the signal catches real errors on your development set before you rely on it.

Conclusion

In this post, we walked through how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to achieve better accuracy at lower cost through model selection on Amazon Bedrock.

Three elements needed to come together for this result: unbiased evaluation to measure honestly, the flexibility to evaluate and switch between model families without re-platforming, and carefully evolved prompts tailored to the domain. Amazon Bedrock provided the foundation. It gave Property Finder access to multiple model families through a single API, inherited AWS governance and security controls, and the ability to adopt new models as they become available without changing their infrastructure.

To get started with model evaluation and selection on Amazon Bedrock, visit the Amazon Bedrock documentation. If you process vision workloads at scale and want help building an unbiased evaluation framework, reach out to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center.

Share your experiences with model evaluation and prompt optimization in the comments.

Additional contributors from AWS include Yousuf Albannai, Amine Sehili, Thomas Ounnas, Aris Tsakpinis, Rafik Soliman, Nikhil Ulhas Pandit, and Sneh Sharma.

item.title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
item.dc:creator: Purna Sanyal
item.description: In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline that produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49x lower cost.
item.content:encoded:
Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it.

In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.

The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies.

The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure

Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably.

A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons:

  1. The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it.
  2. It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops.
  3. Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously.

This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely.

They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge.

Solution overview

Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. The same training pipeline produces fine-tuned models for two deployment targets: the edge and the cloud.

Exowatt implemented this approach on the Qwen3-1.7B model for the first use case, edge alarm triage, then applied the same approach to the Qwen3-14B model for the second use case, cloud energy-market analysis. The company plans to reuse this solution to build smaller, task-specific models across the fleet.

Figure 1: Exowatt fine-tuning and deployment pipeline, spanning the build, cloud-serving, and edge-serving stages

The following seven AWS services power the AI pipeline, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints to manage:

AWS Service Purpose
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Data, manifests, model artifacts, and test sets
Amazon SageMaker AI serverless fine-tuning Every fine-tune run, launched from Public Hub recipes
Amazon SageMaker AI serverless evaluation 2,000 answers per candidate scored as a managed job
SageMaker Model Registry Every completed fine-tune with its evidence and metrics
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B for Cloud EMS, invoked privately from the Cloud EMS service. No idle cost
Amazon Bedrock (Claude, Qwen3)

Paraphrase (three rewrites per answer in the training data) and frontier model benchmarking

Alarm-triage paraphrases use Qwen3-VL-235B on Amazon Bedrock. Energy-market paraphrases use Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock.
AWS Lambda + Amazon EventBridge Serverless-evaluation scorer and a scheduled keep-warm invocation of the custom model

The workflow is organized into three stages:

Model customization (cloud): Exowatt fine-tunes open-weight base models using serverless model customization, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on SageMaker AI. Because serverless training allocates capacity on demand, the team runs multiple experiments per day rather than waiting for self-selected GPU. After evaluation, the best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry.

Edge deployment: For latency-sensitive, connectivity-constrained work such as alarm triage, the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B model is frozen, quantized to the GGUF format, and run with llama.cpp inside Kubernetes pods at the edge using on-site controllers. This path requires no GPU and operates without internet connectivity.

Cloud deployment (elastic): For internet-connected, fleet-level analysis, the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B energy-market model is served through Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, which runs with no idle cost and bills only while the model is active.

Why Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization

Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization service provides a wide selection of open-weight models with ready-made fine-tuning recipes from the SageMaker Public Hub, so the team avoided building and optimizing a custom training container, work that can otherwise take weeks. For Exowatt, this turned fine-tuning from a scarce, scheduled event into a routine, on-demand one. This makes a rapid experimentation-and-test loop practical while keeping experimentation cost low.

Fine-tuning on provisioned GPUs requires choosing a specific instance type, requesting that capacity, waiting for it to become available, running the job, and paying for the instance for as long as it is held. The held time typically includes the idle time between experiments when a dedicated instance is kept running. For a small team running many experiments, this slows down innovation and increases cost. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization automatically manages and orchestrates the infrastructure required to run the fine-tuning job, removing the pain of capacity management, and charges only for the time the fine-tuning job runs.

Use case 1: Edge alarm triage with Qwen3-1.7B

Exowatt sites raise alarms around the clock. A compact on-site model reads each alarm together with the site’s own status and telemetry and returns one of a small fixed set of classifications with cited evidence (such as an offline system, derated component, or sensor mismatch) or an explicit abstention when the evidence is insufficient.

Model selection and training data

The team first tried Qwen3-8B with prompting and guardrails, which plateaued below the target (0.735 macro-F1). A fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B changed that: it outperformed the Qwen3-8B plus prompting setup on this narrow, single-turn task at roughly one-fifth the parameters, while staying small enough for GPU-free edge inference. Thirteen fine-tuned Qwen3-8B candidates across 12 dataset versions never beat the prompted 8B baseline. The smaller model with more varied data did.

The training set was small and curated: 2,522 examples built from 684 verified decisions on generated site scenarios plus 1,838 certified paraphrases that kept each decision fixed while rewriting the prose. The paraphrases were generated by Qwen3-235B on Amazon Bedrock for about $3.72. Each paraphrase was kept only if deterministic checks confirmed that the decision, labels, evidence citations, and every number were unchanged (1,838 of 2,218 candidates passed). One fault family was held out of training entirely, and 320 cases were reserved for testing.

Training and deployment

Training completed in about 32 minutes on SageMaker serverless fine-tuning for roughly $20–$25. Quantized to 8 bits (about 1.71 GiB), the model runs offline in a 6 GiB llama.cpp pod on the site’s existing CPU server. It also runs on a t3.2xlarge instance type.

Use case 2: Cloud energy-market analysis with Qwen3-14B

Dispatchable storage turns timing into an operational decision: each site must continually decide how much stored energy to hold for its load and when to release it, and for grid-connected sites market conditions feed into that choice. The fine-tuned model reads a six-hour packet of live market data (about 90 rows of real-time prices, day-ahead forecasts, and grid notices) and returns one of five market events (such as a price spike or scarcity adder) in about four seconds. Every claim is tied to a specific data row to inform the dispatch strategy.

Why Qwen3-14B

Qwen3-14B was chosen because it is supported by Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, it ships as a SageMaker Public Hub model with a ready LoRA recipe (no custom container or instance type to manage), and at about 28 GiB it is small enough to serve cost-effectively.

Training data and process

Exowatt fine-tuned the model on public Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market data drawn from five years of history (about 163 million rows across 12 tables). The team rule-labeled this data into 25,000 examples (22,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,000 held out for testing). They then expanded the training set to 86,281 rows by having Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock rewrite the prose of each example while its labels and numeric fields stayed fixed.

Training was a single LoRA epoch (rank 16, alpha 32), completed in about 8.5 hours of managed serverless fine-tuning with up to four jobs running at once. The team ran 23 jobs and about 155 hours of managed training in the six days from initial plan to a champion model serving in Cloud EMS.

The decisive improvement came from paraphrase diversity: adding three rewrites per answer lifted macro-F1 from 0.950 to 0.975. The base model scored only 0.415 macro-F1. It produced valid JSON but did not yet know the market. Fine-tuning fixed that.

Deployment

The merged checkpoint was imported to Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import in about 14 minutes. The model runs with no idle cost and bills at $6.86 per hour only while active.

Benchmark results

On the edge alarm-triage task the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B went from a model that couldn’t produce a valid answer to 0.911 macro-F1 with 320 test cases, ahead of every frontier baseline. Applying the identical fine-tune-and-evaluate loop to the energy-market task with 2,000 test cases, the Qwen3-14B reached 0.975 macro-F1, again ahead of the frontier baseline and at a fraction of the cost. In both cases a small, fine-tuned model beat far larger general-purpose models on the specific task.

Both models return strict JSON in which every claim cites a specific input data row. Any unsupported claim is dropped before it reaches an operator, which is what lets the team trust small models in autonomous, physical settings.

The model held 0.968 macro-F1 on a second, later test set.

Business benefits

Faster iteration and faster time to market: Exowatt moved its customized model from experimentation to production in only nine days. This process could have taken months if the team had to build and optimize custom containers and training recipes, provision GPUs, and manage infrastructure. With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, the team trained Qwen3-1.7B in about 32 minutes and Qwen3-14B in about 8.5 hours, with no capacity requests and up to four training jobs running concurrently. For the energy-market use case, Exowatt ran 23 jobs totaling about 155 hours of managed training and moved from the base model to a fine-tuned model serving in Cloud EMS in six days. The merged checkpoint was imported into Amazon Bedrock in about 14 minutes. The end-to-end pipeline used seven AWS serverless services, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints for Exowatt to manage.

Higher accuracy compared to frontier models: Both fine-tuned models beat the larger frontier models on their own task: Qwen3-1.7B at 0.911 macro-F1 (compared to 0.698 for Claude Sonnet 4.6) and Qwen3-14B at 0.975 (compared to 0.625 for Claude Opus 4.7).

Lower cost across both deployments: In the cloud, the Qwen3-14B serves at $0.60 per 1,000 answers versus $29.26 for Claude Opus 4.7 (about 49× lower), with no idle cost and $6.86 per hour only while active on Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import. At the edge, the quantized Qwen3-1.7B runs on the site’s existing CPU with no per-inference cost and no dependency on connectivity.

Grounded, low-risk outputs: Across both models, the evidence fence removed every uncited claim (any evidence citation whose source, field, or value does not literally match the input), and the edge model abstains rather than guesses when unsure. This is what let the team run it autonomously in shadow mode on a cloud-hosted replica of a site.

Lessons learned

For specific tasks, smaller fine-tuned large language models can outperform large frontier models: Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B models each outperformed frontier models on the target task, delivering higher accuracy at a fraction of the cost with significantly smaller models.

Data quality and variety outweigh raw volume and extra epochs: For tightly scoped tasks, data quality mattered more than model size or data volume. On the alarm-triage model, more verified training variety moved macro-F1 from 0.584 (trained on the 684 verified decisions alone) to 0.911 (with the paraphrase-expanded 2,522-row set). Simply running more epochs over the same rows did worse: a control run that trained on the 684 original rows for 11 epochs (the same number of steps) reached only 0.879. Curated data mattered more than dataset size throughout.

Removing the provisioning step changes how a team works: When a training run no longer requires waiting for GPU capacity, fine-tuning shifts from a rare event to a routine, iterative one.

One training pipeline serves two deployment targets: Separating model training from deployment lets Exowatt use the same pipeline for both offline edge deployment and connected fleet-level analysis, simplifying operations and accelerating model deployment in the cloud.

Conclusion

Exowatt now has one reusable AI pipeline that took a task from model specific data preparation to model deployment. Rather than tuning one model for different tasks, Exowatt plans to apply the same fine-tuning principles to different tasks, each with its own data, specific models, and evaluations, across the fleet as new device types and market tasks come online.

The pattern generalizes beyond energy industry segments. AI engineers, data scientists, and customers across industry segments can adopt the same principles. Use Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization as a low-overhead AI pipeline to fine-tune small, task-specific models, then deploy them where the work happens: at the edge when connectivity or latency requires it, and through a managed cloud endpoint such as Amazon SageMaker AI for elastic workloads.

To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization and Amazon Bedrock.

item.title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
item.dc:creator: Kiowa Jackson
item.description: Fleet-wide computer vision needs a model per camera, not one model for the whole fleet. This post presents a working Amazon SageMaker SDK v3 reference architecture that trains, quality-gates, compiles per-camera models with SageMaker Neo, and versions thousands of them, with an AWS Step Functions layer pacing fleet-scale retraining within account quotas.
item.content:encoded:
Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one.

This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute.

The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository.

Solution overview

The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices.

Figure 1: Solution architecture

The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history.

The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved.

The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses.

Prerequisites

To deploy the sample you need the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
  • An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket.
  • An Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository.
  • The SageMaker AI, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon DynamoDB resources in the stacks.
  • Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12, Docker.
  • The AWS CDK CLI version 2.1131.0 or later.

Previous CLI versions fail with a cloud assembly schema mismatch against recent versions of aws-cdk-lib. No service quota increase is needed. The orchestration layer admits at most five pipeline executions at a time by default, which keeps concurrent SageMaker training jobs inside the standard account quota.

If you deploy to an AWS Region other than your CLI default, set all three of AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, and CDK_DEFAULT_REGION on the deploy command itself rather than in your shell profile, for example, AWS_REGION=us-east-2 AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 CDK_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 cdk deploy --all. The CDK CLI, Boto3, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) resolve the Region from overlapping but not identical variable sets, and a mismatch produces confusing partial deployments. Prefixing the command sets all three for that invocation only, so your own default Region is left unchanged.

Defining the training pipeline with SDK v3

The code in this section is excerpted from the CDK application in the repository rather than a standalone script, and it runs during cdk deploy, when the stack synthesizes the pipeline definition. Environment setup and the deploy commands come later, under Deploying and running the sample. SDK v3 reorganized the SageMaker Python SDK into modular packages, and the imports show the new shape of the library:

from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer
from sagemaker.train.configs import InputData, Compute, OutputDataConfig
from sagemaker.core.training.configs import MetricDefinition
from sagemaker.serve.model_builder import ModelBuilder
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.pipeline import Pipeline
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.steps import ProcessingStep, TrainingStep
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.model_step import ModelStep
from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.condition_step import ConditionStep
from sagemaker.core.workflow.conditions import ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo
from sagemaker.core.workflow.functions import JsonGet

Installing sagemaker>=3.0.0,<4 pulls in sagemaker-core, sagemaker-train, sagemaker-serve, and sagemaker-mlops as separate packages. Training configuration that v2 spread across Estimator constructor arguments now lives in typed config objects passed to ModelTrainer. This is the anomaly branch’s trainer, verbatim from the sample:

anomalib_trainer = ModelTrainer(
    training_image=custom_training_image_uri,
    compute=Compute(
        instance_type=training_instance_type.to_string(),
        instance_count=1,
    ),
    base_job_name="cv-pipeline-anomalib-train",
    sagemaker_session=pipeline_session,
    role=role_arn,
    hyperparameters={
        "program": "train_anomalib.py",
        "model_name": "autoencoder",
        "image_size": "256",
        "num_epochs": "3",
        "batch_size": "16",
        "learning_rate": "0.001",
    },
    input_data_config=anomalib_input_data,
    output_data_config=OutputDataConfig(
        s3_output_path=run_prefix("anomalib-training")
    ),
).with_metric_definitions(
    [
        MetricDefinition(
            name="image_auroc",
            regex=r"validation:image_auroc=([0-9]*\.?[0-9]+)",
        ),
    ]
)

anomalib_input_data wires four channels (train, validation, test, pretrained_model) from upstream step properties, and run_prefix scopes every S3 path to the pipeline execution ID so concurrent fleet runs never collide. Both are in the repository.

Two v3 behaviors matter when the pipeline lives inside a CDK application, and neither appears in the changelog as a breaking change. First, SDK v3 validates the pipeline’s execution role against live IAM while building the pipeline definition. This validation happens at synthesis time rather than execution time. A CDK app can’t create the role and the pipeline in one deployment, because the role doesn’t exist yet when the SDK validates it. This is separate from cdk bootstrap, which provisions the CDK toolkit resources once per account and Region and might already be done in your account. The sample’s own two-phase deploy is driven by a context flag that happens to share that name. An initial pass with -c bootstrap=true creates the role, bucket, and ECR repository, and the second pass synthesizes the pipeline against the now-existing role. The role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) embedded in the pipeline definition must also be a concrete string, not an unresolved CDK token.

Second, the v3 role validator simulates ECR pull permissions without a resource ARN, so an execution role scoped to a single ECR repository fails validation even though it would work at runtime. The sample’s role carries a broader ECR grant for this reason.

Lastly, one v3 habit the sample uses: constructing the pipeline with PipelineSession(default_bucket=your_bucket) routes SDK-managed uploads, such as step code, into the pipeline’s own bucket, so every artifact lives in one place and the execution role’s permissions cover a single bucket. (Granting the role access to the SDK’s default bucket works too. This approach is tidier.)

Quality gates that match how defect data behaves

Every trained model is evaluated before registration, and the evaluation runs against the exported ONNX artifact rather than the in-memory PyTorch model. That distinction matters: the artifact you gate is the artifact you ship, so an export problem can never slip a broken model past a healthy-looking training run.

The anomaly branch gates on AUROC of at least 0.8. The classifier branch gates on two metrics at once, and the choice of metrics is shaped by the defining property of defect data: heavy class imbalance. In this sample roughly 90 percent of images are good, which is realistic for a production line. Against that distribution, plain accuracy is meaningless, because a model that predicts “good” for every image scores about 0.9 while catching zero defects. Balanced accuracy, the mean of per-class recall, corrects for that, but it has its own blind spot. A model with perfect recall on good parts and only 20 percent recall on defects still scores (1.0 + 0.2) / 2 = 0.6. So the gate requires balanced accuracy of at least 0.6 and defect recall of at least 0.5, together:

step_check_classifier = ConditionStep(
    name="CheckClassifierQuality",
    conditions=[
        ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo(
            left=JsonGet(
                step_name=step_eval_classifier.name,
                property_file="evaluation",
                json_path="balanced_accuracy",
            ),
            right=min_accuracy,
        ),
        ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo(
            left=JsonGet(
                step_name=step_eval_classifier.name,
                property_file="evaluation",
                json_path="defect_recall",
            ),
            right=min_defect_recall,
        ),
    ],
    if_steps=[step_compile_classifier, step_register_classifier],
    else_steps=[step_fail_classifier],
    depends_on=[step_eval_classifier],
)

A ConditionStep ANDs its conditions, so both must pass. The thresholds are pipeline parameters, adjustable per execution without redeploying. If a gate fails, a FailStep marks the execution failed and that branch’s model never reaches the registry (the two branches gate independently, so the other branch’s model may still register). The fleet keeps serving the previous approved model for that camera.

The training code addresses the same imbalance from the other side. The classifier is a fine-tuned resnet18 with ImageNet weights and a two-class head. At per-camera dataset sizes, fine-tuning pretrained weights is what keeps the model from collapsing onto the majority class. The training code balances training batches with a WeightedRandomSampler using inverse class frequencies, while the loss stays unweighted. Combining a weighted loss with weighted sampling over-corrects toward the minority class.

Compiling for the edge with SageMaker Neo, inside the pipeline

Notice the gate’s if_steps in the preceding code: past the gate, compilation runs first and registration depends on it. Both training scripts export ONNX with dynamic batch axes. The quality gates score those exported artifacts under ONNX Runtime, and then a CompileAnomalibNeo or CompileClassifierNeo step hands the gated artifact to SageMaker Neo. The invariant is gate, then compile, then register. A model only becomes an Approved package if it also compiled for the fleet’s edge target, so the registry never advertises a model the devices cannot run.

The compile step encapsulates three error-prone details. Neo requires the input tarball to contain only the model file, but training jobs emit model.tar.gz with the checkpoint and metrics alongside the ONNX model. The step repackages an ONNX-only tarball first. Neo also requires concrete input shapes while the exports declare a dynamic batch axis, so batch size 1 is pinned in the compilation request. And because pipeline steps can retry, the compilation job name derives deterministically from the execution ID, so a retry resumes polling the job it already started instead of orphaning it.

The target is a pipeline parameter: NeoTargetDevice selects a named device such as jetson_xavier or rasp4b, and its default compiles for the NeoTargetOs/NeoTargetArch platform, LINUX/X86_64 by default. The compiled package contains the optimized compiled.so plus the DLR runtime for loading it. The default output runs on any x86_64 Linux host, so you can validate it before committing to device-specific targets. Compilation itself incurs no charge. You pay for the processing instance that drives it and the S3 storage of the outputs. For compiling an already-registered model for additional device types later, without re-training, the repository includes an ad-hoc script that runs the same flow against the Model Registry.

Per-camera models in the Model Registry

Each branch registers into its own model package group, and every package carries the camera ID and its evaluation metrics. From the sample, with the metrics wiring elided:

classifier_model_builder = ModelBuilder(
    s3_model_data_url=classifier_model_data,
    image_uri=custom_training_image_uri,
    sagemaker_session=pipeline_session,
    role_arn=role_arn,
)
step_register_classifier = ModelStep(
    name="RegisterClassifierModel",
    depends_on=[step_compile_classifier],
    step_args=classifier_model_builder.register(
        model_package_group_name="sm1k-classifier-model-group",
        approval_status="Approved",
        model_metrics=classifier_metrics,
        customer_metadata_properties={"CameraId": camera_id},
    ),
)

Camera identity in customer_metadata_properties is what turns two shared package groups into a fleet catalog. Packages from all cameras live in the same groups, and per-camera history is recovered by filtering on the metadata. Each branch has a fetch step that pages through approved packages newest-first until it finds the requesting camera’s latest model, because ListModelPackages cannot filter on customer metadata server-side. On a camera’s first run the fetch finds nothing and training falls back to its cold-start initialization (ImageNet weights for the classifier, random initialization for the autoencoder). Every later run resumes from that camera’s own prior model, which is what makes frequent, cheap, incremental re-training viable across a fleet.

Note what these registry entries are and are not: they catalog versioned, quality-gated artifacts, but their container reference is the training image, which serves no inference endpoints. They exist for a fleet workflow where a downstream system pulls artifacts and ships them to devices, not for CreateEndpoint.

Orchestrating fleet training requests

Every AWS account has service quotas on concurrent SageMaker training jobs, and each pipeline execution here launches several jobs, so fleet re-training needs pacing. Something has to keep a burst of 500 requests from becoming 500 simultaneous pipeline launches. The sample uses a semaphore, a counter of available slots that works like a parking lot with five spaces. Before the Step Functions state machine starts a pipeline, it takes a slot by atomically incrementing a counter in DynamoDB, with a condition that refuses the increment once the cap is reached:

acquire_semaphore = tasks.DynamoUpdateItem(
    self, "AcquireSemaphore",
    table=semaphore_table,
    key={"LockName": tasks.DynamoAttributeValue.from_string("pipeline-concurrency")},
    update_expression="SET ActiveCount = if_not_exists(ActiveCount, :zero) + :one",
    condition_expression="attribute_not_exists(ActiveCount) OR ActiveCount < :limit",
)

If all slots are taken, the execution waits and retries. When its pipeline finishes, it decrements the counter to release the slot. One detail is worth carrying into your own designs. The DynamoDB condition expression enforces the cap in a single atomic operation, rather than the state machine reading the counter and deciding, which would leave a race window between the read and the write. The repository implements the rest of the operational hardening, including releasing slots on every failure path and forwarding failed executions to Amazon SNS through Amazon EventBridge. Its README covers sizing the wait bounds.

The cap of five is a stack parameter, set low so the sample deploys and runs in any standard account without requesting quota increases. Adjust it to whatever your account’s training-job quotas support. Past a single account’s quotas, scaling fleet training is its own topic. The standard levers are raising the service quotas, spreading training across instance types or Regions, and distributing the fleet across multiple accounts. You can also hold the backlog in SQS and admit work only as capacity frees up. Those choices depend on your fleet’s size and shape. The sample gives you the working skeleton to extend.

Deploying and running the sample

The walkthrough in the repository README is the authoritative version. The following short form starts from a clean checkout and sets up the environment before the first deploy:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline
cd sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cdk bootstrap                                           # once per account/region
cdk deploy SageMakerCVPipelineStack -c bootstrap=true   # roles, bucket, ECR
cdk deploy --all                                        # pipeline + orchestration
./scripts/push_ecr_image.sh                             # build and push training image

By default the pipeline generates synthetic production line images, so you can validate the whole system end to end with no dataset and no data approvals. A full run executes all 13 steps, including both Neo compilations, in about 15 minutes and costs roughly $0.07 in billed ml.m5.xlarge time (US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2), July 2026, on-demand). The orchestration resources together cost well under $0.10 per month at sample scale.

To exercise the pipeline on real images, the repository includes a downloader for the BCCD dataset. The dataset is a collection of 364 annotated blood smear microscopy images originally open sourced on GitHub and reorganized into Pascal VOC format under an MIT license. The same dataset is also distributed by Roboflow as public domain. The script maps platelet presence to the defect class, optionally splits the images per camera to simulate a fleet, and uploads training tarballs to the pipeline bucket. The accompanying notebook runs the full pipeline on the real data and does side-by-side ONNX inference on a normal and an anomalous sample. Treating platelets as defects is an illustrative stand-in for a manufacturing defect distribution, not a clinical claim.

Cleaning up

Model packages are created at pipeline runtime, so AWS CloudFormation cannot delete them. Remove them with the AWS CLI first, then destroy the stacks with cdk destroy --all -c bootstrap=true --force. The README lists the exact commands.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed a working SageMaker SDK v3 reference architecture for the fleet-scale computer vision lifecycle. The architecture includes a dual-branch training pipeline where every model is quality-gated on its exported ONNX artifact, compiled with SageMaker Neo, and only then registered. A Model Registry layout uses camera metadata to turn shared package groups into per-camera warm-startable history, and a Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training within account quotas. For teams whose needs are met by managed options such as Amazon Lookout for Vision, that is the simpler path. This pattern targets the per-camera, fleet-scale constraint that managed options do not cover. The design rules transfer beyond computer vision: gate on balanced accuracy plus minority-class recall rather than accuracy, evaluate and compile the artifact you ship, and make operational failures notify rather than terminate silently.

The sample deploys in minutes and a full validation run costs about seven cents of compute, so a low-cost next step is to clone the repository and run it. From there, point the BCCD downloader at a real bucket, set NeoTargetDevice for your hardware, or size the orchestration bounds to your fleet. For the SDK v3 migration itself, the SageMaker Python SDK documentation and the two-part series announcing the new SDK are the references I kept open throughout.

If you want help adapting this pattern to your production environment, reach out to your AWS account team.

 

About the author

Kiowa Jackson

Kiowa is a Senior Machine Learning Engineer at AWS ProServe. He specializes in visual intelligence systems that combine computer vision with agentic AI, and he brings these to production in the enterprise industrial sector.

item.title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
item.dc:creator: Claudio Mazzoni
item.description: Every time an agent takes a step, it re-reads its entire context before acting. Here is how prompt caching for OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock lets your agent remember, cutting input cost and latency without resending the same tools, instructions, and history every turn.
item.content:encoded:
Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again.

In the movie Groundhog Day, Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years.

Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again.

Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price.

In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent.

What an agent sends to its LLM

Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains:

  • Tool list – The definitions of every function the agent can call. Changes when you ship a new release.
  • Instructions – The developer prompt: rules, persona, policies, examples. Also changes per release.
  • History – Everything that happened in this session so far: the task, the model’s tool calls, and the tool results (which grows every turn).
  • New turn – The latest tool result or user message (which might be different every time).

What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching:

Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn

How prompt caching works under the hood

When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill. During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token.

Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint. You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so.

Turn 1 compared to turn 2

Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question

Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both?

For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically.

New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents.

Hello cached world

The first win is to cache the static part of the prompt: the tools and instructions that stay the same across requests. These examples use your existing Amazon Bedrock client, TOOLS, and task. Replace the shortened INSTRUCTIONS string with your real policies and examples. The reusable prefix must reach 1,024 tokens to qualify.

When caching static content, use explicit mode: choose where the saved prefix ends.

KEY = "support-agent:v7:gpt-6-astra"
INSTRUCTIONS = "Your full support policies and examples..."

# Rendered context: [provider context][TOOLS][INSTRUCTIONS] | [task]
# Cache starts at the beginning; the marker below chooses its end.
resp = client.responses.create(
    model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra",
    store=False,  # Response storage; prompt caching still works.
    include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
    prompt_cache_key=KEY,
    prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"},
    tools=TOOLS,  # Rendered before instructions; keep order stable.
    input=[
        {
            "role": "developer",
            "content": [{
                "type": "input_text",
                "text": INSTRUCTIONS,
                # Save through this whole block, including TOOLS.
                "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"},
            }],
        },
        # User message is processed but not cached.
        {"role": "user", "content": task},
    ],
)

The prompt_cache_key tells the service which requests are meant to share a cache. We come back to how to use it when we get to reading the cache in new sessions. In one of our tests using explicit caching, the roughly 4,000-token tools-and-instructions prefix wrote 4,120 tokens on the first request and read those 4,120 tokens on later requests. The task (or user request) comes after the cache boundary, so this doesn’t trigger a write to the cache.

Keep in mind that prompt caching works only when you pass exactly the same text. Make sure that the agent’s instructions and tool lists are serialized the same way every time. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and other forms of tool delivery need to be indexed to make sure they stay consistent. Keep anything that varies, such as the date, the user’s name, or a request ID, after the cached instructions.

As the content grows and varies (different tools and content), use implicit mode to let the service follow the conversation. Here, the first request has no explicit marker. Its latest eligible message is the user’s task, so the automatic breakpoint comes after that task and covers the tools, instructions, and task together. The mode is shown explicitly in the following example for clarity, even though implicit is the default. Setting store=False leaves conversation history in your application. It doesn’t disable caching.

def ask_with_implicit_cache(history):
    return client.responses.create(
        model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra",
        store=False,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        prompt_cache_key=KEY,
        prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"},
        tools=TOOLS,
        input=history,  # Everything gets cached
    )

history = [
    {"role": "developer", "content": INSTRUCTIONS},
    {"role": "user", "content": task},
]
# Automatic endpoint: the end of the user message.
resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history)

This is useful when the next turn continues the same task. A different task doesn’t match the prefix through the old task, and the implicit write doesn’t necessarily create a separate entry for only the tools and instructions. Use an explicit marker there when you need that shorter shared prefix to be reusable across tasks.

Use both when the agent needs a shared starting point and a growing history. Start with the marked developer block in the following code example and call the function ask_with_implicit_cache. The request-level mode stays implicit. The block-level marker adds an explicit save point after the instructions. The service can also save through the latest eligible message. This keeps the shared prefix available while the conversation grows.

history = [
    {
        "role": "developer",
        "content": [{
            "type": "input_text",
            "text": INSTRUCTIONS,
            "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, 
        }],
    },
    {"role": "user", "content": task},
]
# Still implicit mode, now with an explicit startup save point in the history.
resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history)

Caching conversation history and tool results

The model requests tools by name and supplies their arguments. Your application must execute them. execute_function is a helper you build to route those requests to the matching Python functions and return their results.
