item.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
item.dc:creator: Daniel Quang
item.description: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on the outcome of a whole multi-step task rather than labeled steps. This hands-on guide walks the full pipeline using Wordle: deploying the agent and reward on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, and evaluating at serving settings.
item.content:encoded:
Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome.

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder. The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result.

This post uses Wordle, a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting.

In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models. All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository.

Solution overview

The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect.

Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward

For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word, and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter on the policy model.

Three design points matter for what follows:

  • The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.
  • The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring.
  • The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier.

Supported models and AWS Regions

MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter:

Base model AWS Regions
Amazon Nova 2 Lite US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
GPT-OSS-20B US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned) US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)
Qwen 3.6 27B US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)

We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list.

Pricing

You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model:

  • Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history.
  • Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens.
  • Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter.

The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339:

Dimension Tokens Price per 1M Cost
Prefill 491,616,806 $0.12 $58.99
Sample 159,737,098 $0.30 $47.92
Train 643,308,554 $0.36 $231.59
Total 1,294,662,458 $338.50

The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage. See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites.

  • Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI (npm install -g @aws/agentcore). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs.
  • botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the AgentRFT CreateJob operation.
  • Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1.
  • An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because CreateJob rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN.

Step 1: Create the IAM roles

MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention.

Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically.

Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy.

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Principal": {"Service": "job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com"},
        "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }]
}

Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com, not sagemaker.amazonaws.com. With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries.

Step 2: Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Clone the sample repository, set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/aws-targets.json, and deploy:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle
cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle
agentcore validate
agentcore deploy

The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job.

Figure 2: The Wordle agent runtime in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console with status Ready

The runtime reads two environment variables from agentcore.json. REASONING_EFFORT=low sets reasoning_effort on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word.

Figure 3: Runtime environment variables showing REASONING_EFFORT set to low

The agent is one file, main.py. Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward:

app = BedrockAgentCoreApp()

@app.entrypoint  # outermost: starts the HTTP server AgentCore invokes
@sagemaker_rft_handler  # reports the returned reward to SageMaker AI
def handle_rollout(payload):
    prompt, answer = parse_task(payload["prompt"])
    game = WordleGame(answer)

    @tool
    def guess_word(guess: str) -> str:
        """Submit a 5-letter Wordle guess and get feedback."""
        return game.guess(guess)

    agent = Agent(model=build_model(), system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT, tools=[guess_word])
    agent(prompt)
    return {"reward": game.final_reward()}

Important: The sagemaker_rft_handler decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with BedrockAgentCoreApp and @app.entrypoint, with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds.

Step 3: Verify the runtime

Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/payload.json:

{
  "prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"beach\", \"id\": \"smoke-test\"}",
  "metadata": {
    "jobArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:111122223333:job/AgentRFT/smoke-test",
    "rolloutId": "r1"
  }
}

The fake job ARN is expected to fail, and the way it fails is the proof. Put your own account ID into it first: for a job ARN in another account, the service returns a 403 before it checks whether the job exists, which looks like a broken IAM setup. From the Wordle directory, run:

ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
sed "s/111122223333/$ACCOUNT/" payload.json > /tmp/payload.json

aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-agent-runtime \
  --agent-runtime-arn <RUNTIME_ARN> \
  --runtime-session-id smoke-test-$(date +%s)000000000000000 \
  --payload fileb:///tmp/payload.json /dev/stdout

In the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch logs, you see the agent parse the prompt, authenticate to the Job Runtime endpoint, and receive a 400 error reading “Could not find job.” That failure confirms that parsing, authentication, and error reporting work. The command itself prints {“reward”: -1.5}, because the agent never reached the policy model. A 403 reading “not authorized to access this resource” means the job ARN still names another account. A 30-second timeout instead means the HTTP server is not starting (see the Important note in Step 2).

Step 4: Prepare the dataset

The MTRL dataset has no target responses, transcripts, or labels. Each row is one task for the agent to attempt. Here are the first three rows of the training file:

{"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"riser\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0000\"}"}
{"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"swoon\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0001\"}"}
{"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"dirty\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0002\"}"}

The service reads the prompt column (or the first column) and passes the string to your agent verbatim, without parsing it. We made the string a small JSON object with three fields:

  • prompt: the instruction the agent shows the policy model, identical on every row.
  • answer: the secret word. Only the environment and the reward function use it. The policy model never sees it.
  • id: a row ID for tracing a rollout in the logs back to its source row.

The sample repository’s make_dataset.py draws 640 training words (five full batches of 128) and 128 validation words from the answer list with no overlap, so the validation solve rate measures generalization. The service also accepts Apache Parquet, JSON arrays, and CSV. Upload both files to Amazon S3:

uv run python make_dataset.py
aws s3 cp training-data.jsonl s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/train/
aws s3 cp validation-data.jsonl s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/validation/

Because the service never inspects the prompt string, a production task can pack a full message list, tool configuration, or reward specification into it. See the MTRL documentation for examples, including how to protect sensitive content in the string.

Step 5: Launch the training job

The launcher uses the MultiTurnRLTrainer class from the sagemaker-train SDK. Point it at the runtime ARN from Step 2, the role from Step 1, the datasets from Step 4, and an MLflow app for metrics. The MLflow app is required, so if you don’t have one, create it first with aws sagemaker create-mlflow-app:

uv run python run_mtrl_training.py \
  --model openai-reasoning-gpt-oss-20b \
  --agent-runtime-arn <RUNTIME_ARN> \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT>:role/<JOB_ROLE> \
  --train-dataset s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/train/training-data.jsonl \
  --val-dataset s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/validation/validation-data.jsonl \
  --s3-output-path s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/output/ \
  --mlflow-app-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:<REGION>:<ACCOUNT>:mlflow-app/<APP_ID>

The launcher overrides three hyperparameters and leaves every other one at the gpt-oss-20b default. It sets sampling_max_tokens to 8192, the service maximum, because at the default of 4096 gpt-oss often ran out of tokens while reasoning, before its first tool call. It sets max_epochs to 20 and max_steps to 100: 640 rows at the default global_batch_size of 128 is 5 steps per epoch, and with the default group_size of 8, each step plays 1,024 games. The job moves through Starting, Downloading, and Pending before reaching Training. After it’s training, your AgentCore runtime begins receiving rollout invocations.

Important: Don’t redeploy the agent while a job is running. Redeploying restarts the runtime, in-flight rollouts see no sampling requests, and the service fails the entire job.

Step 6: Monitor training in MLflow

The service logs reward, token, and turn statistics at every step and runs validation every val_every steps. The metric to watch is val/reward/pass_at_1, the fraction of held-out words solved. Every solve scores at least 1.01, so it clears the service’s success_threshold of 1.0 and pass@1 counts it. The following chart is built from this run’s MLflow history:

Figure 4: Training curves for the 100-step run, with mean reward per game on the left and validation solve rate on the right

Training reward climbs to about +0.57 within 15 steps and holds there. Validation reward stays lower, mostly because of temperature 1.0 versus 0 rather than overfitting (see Step 7). The validation solve rate jumps from 2 to 31 percent in the first 10 steps, then moves between 35 and 48 percent. With 128 words, those swings are mostly noise. We did not test whether more steps help at serving settings.

The runtime’s OpenTelemetry traces in CloudWatch record every model turn and tool call. Here is one game the trained model played during an evaluation job (medium effort, temperature 1.0), with the reasoning trimmed. The secret word was PASTE:

[model] Reasoning: [...] "CRANE" has 5 distinct letters: C,R,A,N,E. [...]
We'll guess "CRANE".
Tool call: guess_word(guess="CRANE")
[tool] Guess 1/6: CRANE -> C=gray, R=gray, A=yellow, N=gray, E=green
Current Knowledge:
- Correct Position (Green): _ _ _ _ E
- In Word, Wrong Position (Yellow): 'A' (at least 1)
- Not in Word (Gray): C, N, R
- Guesses Remaining: 5
[model] Reasoning: [...] "ALIVE": ends with E, includes A. Letters not C,N,R.
Tool call: guess_word(guess="ALIVE")
[tool] Guess 2/6: ALIVE -> A=yellow, L=gray, I=gray, V=gray, E=green
[model] Reasoning: [...] So positions not 1 or 3 for A. Positions left: 2,4
for A. [...] We might guess "HASTE"? [...]
Tool call: guess_word(guess="HASTE")
[tool] Guess 3/6: HASTE -> H=gray, A=green, S=green, T=green, E=green
[model] Reasoning: We have the word: _ASTE. [...] "PASTE" is a word. PASTE
fits. Also "WASTE" also fits [...] Choose "PASTE" maybe.
Tool call: guess_word(guess="PASTE")
[tool] Guess 4/6: PASTE --- all green. Correct, you solved it!

A trained-model rollout from the AgentCore runtime traces. The model keeps green letters in place, never reuses a gray letter, and uses each yellow letter to rule out positions, though nothing in the training data showed it how.

Step 7: Evaluate the trained model at serving settings

When the job completes, its page in SageMaker AI Studio shows the status and the model package group that holds the trained model. DescribeJob, with JobCategory set to AgentRFT, returns the output model package ARN and the billable token counts.

Figure 5: The completed training job in SageMaker AI Studio on the Jobs, Training, Multi-turn RL tab

An evaluation job (JobCategory set to AgentRFTEvaluation) plays your evaluation prompts through the same AgentCore runtime and reward, on the base model or the trained package, and logs eval/reward/pass_at_1 to MLflow. Unlike training validation, you can set the temperature. The repository’s launcher runs evaluations back to back, because the default quota allows one evaluation job at a time (you can request an increase):

uv run python run_mtrl_eval.py --runs base:1.0 trained:1.0 \
  --model-package-arn <OUTPUT_MODEL_PACKAGE_ARN> \
  --agent-runtime-arn <RUNTIME_ARN> \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT>:role/<JOB_ROLE> \
  --dataset s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/validation/validation-data.jsonl \
  --s3-output-path s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/eval/ \
  --mlflow-app-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:<REGION>:<ACCOUNT>:mlflow-app/<APP_ID>

Figure 6: Reasoning effort and sampling temperature at each stage, where the training job fixes validation at temperature 0 and the deployed effort while evaluation jobs let you choose

Each 128-word evaluation took four to seven minutes. Reasoning effort comes from the agent’s environment variables, so to change it you edit REASONING_EFFORT, redeploy, and evaluate. We evaluated both models at low and medium effort and at temperature 0 and 1.0:

Figure 7: Base model versus trained model under four decoding settings, with solve rate on the left and mean reward per game on the right

The gray segment of each bar is the base model and the blue segment is the gain from training. The low-effort, temperature-0 pair is the training job’s validation at steps 0 and 100. The medium-effort, temperature-1.0 trained result is the mean of two runs (80 and 88 percent).

At temperature 0, both models often end the game without a solve, at either effort. With sampling on, medium effort adds 15 points for the trained model and 46 for the base model. The adapter adds 14–54 points in every setting, so what training taught transfers across settings.

The training job’s own validation curve in MLflow told a different story: it peaked at 48 percent at step 90 and ended at 37 percent, scored at temperature 0. The hyperparameters reference recommends temperature 0 for evaluation because greedy decoding makes curves deterministic and comparable across runs. We report temperature 1.0 because that’s how we serve the model. At medium effort and temperature 1.0, the trained model solves 84 percent of held-out words, up from 61 percent for the base model.

Tip: Evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The training curve says this adapter ends at 37 percent. At serving settings it solves 84 percent. The evaluation jobs that show this cost about $1.20 in tokens and took about an hour.

Step 8: Clean up

Training and evaluation jobs stop billing when they complete, but the AgentCore runtime, its IAM role, the MLflow app, and the S3 objects persist. From the project directory:

# 1. Agent runtime and its execution role. remove all resets the project config;
# the next deploy sees the empty state and tears down the deployed resources.
cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle
agentcore remove all
agentcore deploy

# 2. MLflow app
aws sagemaker delete-mlflow-app --arn arn:aws:sagemaker:<REGION>:<ACCOUNT>:mlflow-app/<APP_ID>

# 3. Datasets, job output, and evaluation output
aws s3 rm s3://<YOUR_BUCKET>/wordle-mtrl/ --recursive

Because agentcore remove all rewrites the files under agentcore/, run git checkout -- agentcore/ if you want to redeploy later. Deleting the AgentCore-Wordle-default CloudFormation stack removes the same resources and leaves the files alone. The training job role and the model packages are not billed.

Deep dive: Designing the reward

Our reward needed one revision, and the mistake is a common one.

The first design summed the per-guess scoring from the wordle-lora-rl project over the whole game. That scoring works there because each guess is an independent training sample. Summed into one reward per game, it produced two inversions we found only by reading traces:

  • A lost game paid positive reward. Six turns of bonuses added up to about +0.49.
  • Solving on turn 1 scored below solving on turn 3. A first-guess solve earned +0.99 and a third-guess solve earned +1.61, because the extra turns collected more bonuses.

The fix separates a dominant outcome term from a small, bounded shaping term:

reward = outcome + w * clip(shaping, -1, 1), w = 0.04 if solved, else 0.15

The outcome term is set entirely by how the game ended:

Outcome Value
Solved on guess n 1.05 + 0.5 * (6 – n) / 5, so 1.55 on guess 1 down to 1.05 on guess 6
Played all six guesses, unsolved -0.5
Never made a valid guess -1.5

The shaping term is that per-guess scoring, summed over the game:

  • Penalties for contradicting a known green, yellow, or gray letter, for repeating a guess, and for words outside the dictionary.
  • An entropy bonus for a strong opening word.
  • Bonuses for trying new letters and for shrinking the set of remaining possibilities.

The sum is clipped to [-1, 1] and scaled by 0.04 for a solve and 0.15 for a loss, so it separates games with the same outcome but never moves a game into another tier. With typical shaping values:

Scenario Reward
Solve on guess 1 +1.550
Solve on guess 3 +1.375
Solve on guess 6 +1.069
Lost after six guesses -0.427
Never made a valid guess -1.500

A faster solve now always beats a slower one, every solve beats every loss, and never playing is the worst outcome. Our first fix used a single weight of 0.15, which let a guess-3 solve with full shaping (+1.45) outscore a guess-2 solve with the minimum (+1.25). Adjacent guess counts are 0.1 apart, so a smaller solve weight of 0.04 removes the overlap, and the worst solve (+1.01) still clears the 1.0 success threshold. Shaping still matters because GRPO learns from reward variance within a group, so two lost games that differ in clue consistency still teach the model something. As the SageMaker AI documentation advises, start with an outcome-based reward, add shaping sparingly, and check the reward on real trajectories.

Deep dive: What went wrong, in the order you will hit it

Each of these cost at least one training run.

  • Bearer tokens under concurrency. Minting a token with a fresh botocore session per call starved the credential provider at 32 concurrent rollouts, and caching tokens for an hour returned 403 errors as credentials rotated. The fix is one self-refreshing session, a short cache, and a re-sign on 403.
  • A rollout that never reaches the policy model fails the whole job. When every model call in a rollout failed authentication, the service ended the job with “No sampling requests were received.” Returning an error status fails it too, so always return a reward. A game where the model is sampled but never makes a valid guess is fine: it scores -1.5, and the 100-step run had 51 of them in about 105,000 rollouts.
  • Tool calls drift into plain text. At too high a learning rate, the model wrote tool calls as text, every rollout got the same floor reward, and the gradient vanished. The agent now recovers guesses from raw text with a small formatting penalty.
  • The plateau. Training reward stopped rising after about step 15 and validation stopped improving after about step 30, though at temperature 0 validation understates the model (Step 7). A curriculum that seeds games with prior guesses, or more rollouts per word than the default group_size of 8, is what we would try next.

Conclusion

MTRL on SageMaker AI trains a model on the outcome of a whole episode. That fits agentic tasks, where the right trajectory is unknown and only the result can be scored. We used a single episode-level reward. When intermediate steps can be scored too, MTRL also accepts one reward per turn through the UpdateReward API. In this post, an open-weight 20B model reached an 84 percent solve rate at serving settings, up from 61 percent, for about $339 in training tokens and about $79 in AgentCore runtime usage. The 37 percent the training curve reports is an artifact of how the training job scores validation, so evaluate at the settings you will serve at.

The same pipeline applies to internal procedures, tools, and workflows that public models were never trained on.

To get started, clone the sample repository, follow the preceding steps, and run the smoke test in Step 3 before committing GPU time. For the underlying APIs, see the SageMaker AI MTRL documentation.

item.title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
item.dc:creator: Lauren Eterno
item.description: Updating a SageMaker AI endpoint that has Application Auto Scaling registered makes AWS CloudFormation and AWS CDK deployments fail. This post shows how to build a reusable AWS CDK construct with CloudFormation custom resources that deregisters and re-registers auto scaling automatically, so you can update the endpoint and its scaling in a single deployment.
item.content:encoded:
Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources.

In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention.

Why this problem occurs

When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue.

Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered

CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error:

The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated.

SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources.

Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration

If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong.

Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters

If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists:

Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/<name>/variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found.

This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover.

Solution overview

You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is:

  1. Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues.
  2. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration.
  3. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target.
  4. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy.

Figure 1: Custom resource orchestration of SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling around a CDK-managed endpoint update.

Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy use the CDK provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. Each custom resource has an on_event handler that returns immediately and an is_complete handler. The provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on an interval (every 30 seconds) until its readiness check passes. The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour for Register Scalable Target, 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy) bounds the wait, so it isn’t limited by the timeout of any single Lambda invocation.

A ConfigHash property on each custom resource forces CloudFormation to re-invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes. The endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters are defined together because a single ConfigHash drives the auto scaling orchestration.

While the construct defines three custom resources, the deployed stack contains more than three Lambda functions. Each custom resource is backed by a CDK cr.Provider, and the provider framework generates its own helper Lambda functions. A synchronous provider (Deregister) adds one framework function. An asynchronous provider (Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy) adds three (onEvent, isComplete, and onTimeout) plus an AWS Step Functions state machine that drives the waiter. As a result, the deployed stack contains three custom resources, two Step Functions state machines, and twelve Lambda functions. Five of the resources hold the construct’s own handler code (one for Deregister, and an on_event and is_complete pair for each asynchronous resource), with the remaining seven generated by the provider framework. You don’t write or maintain the framework-generated functions, but they are present in the stack and worth accounting for when you review the deployed resources.

Walkthrough

In this walkthrough, you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with auto scaling using the provided example stack, then verify that configuration updates work correctly.

The walkthrough includes the following steps:

  1. Clone the repository and install dependencies.
  2. Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings.
  3. Deploy and verify.
  4. Test an update.

The source code is available in the linked GitHub repository.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions for Amazon SageMaker AI, AWS Lambda, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Application Auto Scaling, and Amazon CloudWatch.
  • AWS CDK v2 installed.
  • Python 3.12 or later.
  • uv for Python dependency management.
  • A SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and a container image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), or a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm container.

Clone the repository and install dependencies

  1. Clone the repository: 
    git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling.git
cd sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling
  2. Install dependencies: 
    uv sync

Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings

The endpoint and auto scaling settings are defined together in config/config.yaml because a single config_hash drives the auto scaling orchestration. A change to either section triggers the full sequence.

Edit config/config.yaml with your values:

endpoint:
  endpoint_name: "my-model-endpoint"
  image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:latest"
  model_data_url: "s3://my-bucket/models/model.tar.gz"
  instance_type: "ml.m5.large"
  initial_instance_count: 1
  environment: {}
autoscaling:
  min_capacity: 1
  max_capacity: 10
  target_value: 100
  scale_in_cooldown: 600
  scale_out_cooldown: 120

The endpoint parameters map to the SageMaker AI CreateModel and CreateEndpointConfig APIs. The auto scaling parameters map to the Application Auto Scaling RegisterScalableTarget and PutScalingPolicy APIs.

Deploy and verify

  1. Bootstrap your AWS environment if you haven’t already: 
    uv run cdk bootstrap
  2. Deploy the stack: 
    uv run cdk deploy InferenceStack

CloudFormation creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, then runs the three custom resources in sequence to register auto scaling.

  1. Verify that the deployment registered the scalable target: 
    aws application-autoscaling describe-scalable-targets
--service-namespace sagemaker
--resource-ids endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic
  2. Verify that the deployment applied the scaling policy: 
    aws application-autoscaling describe-scaling-policies
--service-namespace sagemaker
--resource-id endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic

Test an update

Change a value in config/config.yaml, for example, update the instance type from ml.m5.large to ml.m5.xlarge, and redeploy:

uv run cdk deploy InferenceStack

After the deployment completes, verify that auto scaling is still registered and has the updated values:

aws application-autoscaling describe-scalable-targets
--service-namespace sagemaker
--resource-ids endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic

Integrating with an existing stack

Use the example stack if you’re starting fresh or want a reference implementation. Use the construct directly if you already have a CDK stack with SageMaker AI resources.

To integrate with an existing stack, copy the sagemaker_autoscaling/constructs/ directory into your project and add the construct alongside your endpoint resources:

import json
from sagemaker_autoscaling.constructs.sagemaker_autoscaling_construct import (
    AutoscalingConfig,
    SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct,
    SagemakerAutoscalingProps,
)

# Both endpoint and auto scaling values must be in config_hash so that
# a change to either triggers the auto scaling orchestration.
config_hash = json.dumps({
    "endpoint": {
        "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:latest",
        "modelDataUrl": "s3://my-bucket/models/model.tar.gz",
        "instanceType": "ml.m5.large",
        "initialInstanceCount": 1,
    },
    "autoscaling": {
        "minCapacity": 1,
        "maxCapacity": 10,
        "targetValue": 100,
        "scaleInCooldown": 600,
        "scaleOutCooldown": 120,
    },
})

SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct(
    self, "Autoscaling",
    props=SagemakerAutoscalingProps(
        endpoint=your_endpoint,  # your CfnEndpoint
        autoscaling=AutoscalingConfig(
            min_capacity=1,
            max_capacity=10,
            target_value=100,
            scale_in_cooldown=600,
            scale_out_cooldown=120,
        ),
        config_hash=config_hash,
    ),
)

How the construct works

This section walks through the key implementation details of SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct.

Deregister

The Deregister custom resource calls deregister_scalable_target before the endpoint update. It handles ObjectNotFoundException for first deployments where no scalable target exists:

def handler(event, context):
    resource_id = event["ResourceProperties"]["ResourceId"]
    if event["RequestType"] in ("Create", "Update"):
        try:
            client.deregister_scalable_target(
                ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
                ResourceId=resource_id,
                ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
            )
        except client.exceptions.ObjectNotFoundException:
            pass  # No scalable target on first deploy
    return {"PhysicalResourceId": f"deregister-{resource_id}"}

The dependency is established in CDK:

props.endpoint.node.add_dependency(deregister)

Register Scalable Target

Even though CloudFormation treats the endpoint resource as complete once the update is accepted, the scalable target can only be registered after the endpoint reaches InService. Rather than block a single Lambda invocation on that wait, Register Scalable Target uses the provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. The on_event handler returns immediately, and the provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on query_interval until the endpoint is InService. The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour) bounds the wait, not the timeout of any single Lambda invocation:

def handler(event, context):
    props = event["ResourceProperties"]
    resource_id = props["ResourceId"]
    endpoint_name = resource_id.split("/")[1]
    if event["RequestType"] == "Delete":
        return {"IsComplete": True}
    status = sm_client.describe_endpoint(EndpointName=endpoint_name)["EndpointStatus"]
    if status == "Failed":
        raise Exception("Endpoint in Failed state")
    if status != "InService":
        return {"IsComplete": False}
    as_client.register_scalable_target(
        ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
        ResourceId=resource_id,
        ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
        MinCapacity=int(props["MinCapacity"]),
        MaxCapacity=int(props["MaxCapacity"]),
    )
    return {"IsComplete": True}

On stack deletion, the on_event handler deregisters the scalable target to clean up.

Attach Scaling Policy

There is a brief window after RegisterScalableTarget returns where the target isn’t yet queryable. Attach Scaling Policy uses the same asynchronous completion pattern: the on_event handler returns immediately, and the is_complete handler reports completion only once the scalable target is queryable, at which point it applies the policy. The provider’s total_timeout (15 minutes) bounds the wait:

def handler(event, context):
    props = event["ResourceProperties"]
    resource_id = props["ResourceId"]
    if event["RequestType"] == "Delete":
        return {"IsComplete": True}
    resp = client.describe_scalable_targets(
        ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
        ResourceIds=[resource_id],
        ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
    )
    if not resp.get("ScalableTargets"):
        return {"IsComplete": False}
    client.put_scaling_policy(
        PolicyName=props["PolicyName"],
        ServiceNamespace="sagemaker",
        ResourceId=resource_id,
        ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount",
        PolicyType="TargetTrackingScaling",
        TargetTrackingScalingPolicyConfiguration=json.loads(props["ScalingPolicyConfig"]),
    )
    return {"IsComplete": True}

On stack deletion, the on_event handler deletes the scaling policy to clean up.

Cleaning up

To avoid incurring future charges, delete the resources:

uv run cdk destroy InferenceStack

This removes the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, model, Lambda functions, IAM roles, Amazon CloudWatch alarms created by the target tracking scaling policy, and deregisters the scalable target.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how to use a reusable CDK construct to deregister and register auto scaling automatically to orchestrate SageMaker AI endpoint updates. The construct uses three CloudFormation custom resources with explicit dependency ordering and a ConfigHash property to keep auto scaling intact across deployments.

To get started, clone the sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling repository and follow the setup instructions. The repository includes an example stack you can deploy directly, or you can integrate the construct into your existing CDK stack.

For more information about Application Auto Scaling for SageMaker AI, see Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker AI models. For more information about CloudFormation custom resources, see Custom resources in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide.

About the author

Lauren Eterno

Lauren is an Associate Delivery Consultant with Amazon Web Services specializing in AI/ML. She works with customer teams to design, build, deploy, and scale machine learning and generative AI solutions. She holds a B.S. in Data Science & Analytics and an M.S. in Computer Science from Case Western Reserve University.

item.title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
item.dc:creator: Amit Makashir
item.description: Amazon Quick Sight layer maps now support Point and LineString geometry from the same GeoJSON workflow, so you can plot store locations and the routes between them. This post covers the dataset and GeoJSON structure layer maps require, when to choose points or lines, and techniques for viewport control, layering geometries, and dynamic GeoJSON updates.
item.content:encoded:
With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched, you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them.

Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString. Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports.

Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick, is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies.

In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically.

Dataset structure considerations

A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized.

Prerequisites

The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight:

  • A GeoJSON file describing your geometry.
  • A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions.
  • A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file.
  • The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB.

Structure of the GeoJSON file

GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines.

{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [{
    "type": "Feature",
    "geometry": {
      "type": "Point",
      "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6]
    },
    "properties": { "prop0": "value0" }
  }, {
    "type": "Feature",
    "geometry": {
      "type": "LineString",
      "coordinates": [
        [88.2, 22.4],
        [88.9, 23.1],
        [89.5, 22.8],
        [90.1, 23.6]
      ]
    },
    "properties": { "prop0": "value0" }
  }]
}

The structure of the file is as follows:

  • FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array.
  • Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key.
  • geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates. The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point, and an ordered list of positions for a LineString.

Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON

In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize, which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field, which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer.

Example: LineString layer

Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows:

{
  "type": "Feature",
  "geometry": {
    "type": "LineString",
    "coordinates": [
      [-73.7781, 40.6413],
      [-85.5627, 40.6407],
      [-97.1415, 39.4569],
      [-108.1612, 37.1753],
      [-118.4085, 33.9416]
    ]
  },
  "properties": { "route_id": "JFK-LAX" }
}

The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information:

Figure 1: Dataset row for the JFK-LAX route, keyed by route_id

The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines.

Figure 2: The JFK-LAX route drawn as a LineString layer

Example: Point layer

Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows:

{
  "type": "Feature",
  "geometry": {
    "type": "Point",
    "coordinates": [-73.9490, 40.7447]
  },
  "properties": { "store_id": "S-109" }
}

The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information:

Figure 3: Dataset row for a store, keyed by store_id

The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points.

Figure 4: A store plotted as a Point layer

Lines on layer map visuals

Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence.

Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as flight paths, delivery routes, shipping lanes, or pipeline segments. The visual draws each path from the coordinates in your GeoJSON file rather than generating it from your data at load time. A field from your joined dataset can determine the line color encoding, so you can group routes by whatever that field represents. In addition to color, you can customize lines with width and opacity controls to adjust visual prominence and clarity on the map. The join key in the GeoJSON properties object ties each LineString to the dataset row behind its tooltip and color.

For example, an airport operations team might map the flights leaving New York (JFK) on a given day. The GeoJSON file holds one LineString per route, keyed by a route ID that joins to the dataset. Each line starts at JFK and ends at its destination, such as Los Angeles, Chicago, or Miami. The dataset supplies the origin, destination, and carrier that show up in the tooltip.

Figure 5: Flights leaving JFK drawn as LineString routes to multiple destinations

Points on layer map visuals

Amazon Quick Sight offers a native point map visual type that geocodes location names automatically and refreshes with your SPICE schedule or Direct Query connection. It supports dynamic point sizing, color encoding, and point styles such as cluster points and heatmap density gradients. It works best with data that changes frequently and where you want the map to respond to those changes visually.

With the added support for GeoJSON point layers in layer map visuals, Quick Sight now offers a second point mapping capability with a few key differences. Layer map visual points use a uniform marker size and don’t support geocoding, so you provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file. In return, you can control the viewport precisely, locking the map to an exact geographic region, and disabling panning and zooming.

The following table summarizes the key differences:

Feature Point map Layer map visual points
Data source Latitude/longitude values or geolocation names in your dataset GeoJSON Point features joined to your dataset by a shared key
Geocoding Recognizes city, county, state, country, and postal code automatically Not available. Must provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file
Location updates Mapping updates automatically with SPICE refreshes or Direct Query as location values change Visual uses a static GeoJSON file for point locations. Requires manual re-upload or API call to update geometry
Viewport Auto-fits to your data, panning and zooming always enabled Auto-fits by default, can configure if panning and zooming is allowed
Appearance Size and color can be encoded from the dataset. Point style configuration available (basic, cluster, heatmap) Customizable uniform marker size, fill opacity, border color and thickness. Color can be encoded from the dataset

Choose layer map visual points when:

  • You require a locked, non-scrollable viewport.
  • Your locations are fixed and curated (such as regional offices, distribution centers, retail stores) rather than changing with each data refresh.
  • You plan to combine points with other geometry types (covered in the advanced use cases section).

Consider a retail brand whose regional managers use a Quick Sight dashboard to track store performance across a metro area. The GeoJSON file contains a Point feature for each store with a store ID property that joins to the dataset. The dataset holds the metrics (store type, monthly revenue, daily foot traffic) that drive the tooltip and color encoding. You position the map at the zoom level covering the metro area, then disable map navigation so the map renders at a consistent view on every load. Managers can’t accidentally zoom out to a national or global view.

Figure 6: Store locations as points with map navigation disabled to lock the metro-area view

Advanced use cases

The previous sections cover a standard layer map setup. Use the following techniques when you need more control over what readers see, want to combine geometry types in a single view, or need geometry that changes over time.

Controlling the viewport

When you need to control the viewport in layer map visuals, you can pan and zoom to the view you want manually. Then disable map navigation to lock it in place. For use cases where you need more precise boundaries or programmatic control, you can set the exact viewport coordinates through the visual definition using the Quick Sight APIs.

The layer map visual stores its viewport configuration in the MapState property within ChartConfiguration. This property accepts two fields:

  • Bounds: The geographic coordinates defining the minimum visible area (North, South, East, West).
  • MapNavigation: ENABLED or DISABLED to control whether readers can pan and zoom.

Although the bounds property is not exposed on the console, you can set these bounds when working with the dashboard definition JSON for programmatic asset management. For example, to define the bounds, modify the MapState block in the visual definition, then call the CreateDashboard or UpdateDashboard APIs.

The bounds define the minimum area that is guaranteed to be visible. The map zooms to make sure this entire area fits within the visual container. For the tightest fit with minimal extra space added to the map, match the aspect ratio of your bounds to the shape of your visual container.

Layering geometries

For use cases that require combining multiple geometry types into a single view, you can layer visuals on top of each other. For example, the following screenshot demonstrates plotting customer locations as points within US regional boundaries defined by polygons. This composition shows which territories have the highest customer density and can be used to correlate with other metrics present in the dataset like performance.

Figure 7: Customer points layered within polygon regional boundaries

This second example demonstrates combining points as stops along a delivery route path. The LineString draws the planned route, and Point features mark each scheduled stop along the way.

Figure 8: A delivery route drawn as a LineString with Point markers for each stop

To layer geometries, you stack multiple layer map visuals on top of each other, following these steps:

  1. Use free-form layout: Change the sheet layout setting to free-form so that visuals can overlap and stack.
  2. Create two layer map visuals: Create the two layer map visuals that you combine into a single view, such as one using a Point GeoJSON file and one using a LineString GeoJSON file.
  3. Use matching bounds: Using the approach previously described for controlling the viewport, verify all layer map visuals use identical bounds to have the same underlying map view.
  4. Disable panning and zooming: For each layer map visual, disable the panning and zooming under Map options so that alignment stays the same.
  5. Hide the base map and background on upper layer: Set the upper visual’s background to hidden under Display settings and disable the base map under Map options.
  6. Stack the visuals: Move the top visual on top of the base layer using drag-and-drop or by matching precise size and position coordinates under Display settings.

Layer ordering follows the visual stacking order in the free-form layout. To change a visual’s position in the stack, choose the menu icon (three dots) on the visual, then choose Send backward or Bring forward. Readers can access the tooltip of the topmost visual, so place the layer that readers need details from on top. Each sheet supports up to five layer map visuals.

Dynamically updating GeoJSON

Unlike other Quick Sight visuals where data refreshes through SPICE or Direct Query, layer map geometry lives in the GeoJSON file itself. When your dataset refreshes on schedule, the metrics update (for example, colors change and tooltip values refresh), but the geometry remains at its original position.

To update what appears on the map, like a new route, new point locations, or updated boundaries, you need to update the GeoJSON file and republish the dashboard. You can replace a GeoJSON file manually through the Quick Sight console by editing the layer map visual within the Analysis and uploading a new file. This works for infrequent changes such as updating territory boundaries quarterly or adding a new store location.

For automated, on-demand, or dynamic updates, the process involves Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the Quick Sight APIs outlined in the following steps:

  1. Upload the new GeoJSON to Amazon S3: Generate your updated geometry and save it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Custom solutions can use other AWS services such as Amazon Location Service to create the GeoJSON files.
  2. Reference the file on the dashboard definition: The dashboard definition contains a StaticFiles array with a SpatialStaticFile entry for each GeoJSON file. Modify the file reference to the S3 location of your updated file entry for each GeoJSON file.
  3. Call the UpdateDashboard API: Submit the updated definition with the new file reference using the UpdateDashboard API.
  4. Call the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API: Publish the change so it is visible to dashboard readers with the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API.

The following example uses this pattern to support on-demand map updates in an embedded dashboard to generate optimal routes between locations and waypoints. Although outside the scope of this post, this represents an advanced use case that combines each of the preceding approaches.

Figure 9: On-demand route generation in an embedded dashboard

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to use Point and LineString geometry in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps to plot specific locations and the routes between them. We covered the GeoJSON structure and dataset join that layer maps require, and compared layer map points with the native point map. We also walked through advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering separate visuals into one view, and refreshing GeoJSON files with Amazon S3 and the Quick Sight APIs.

To learn more about layered maps, refer to the Amazon Quick Sight layered maps documentation. Visit the Amazon Quick Community to connect with peers and stay updated on the newest features and resources.

 

About the authors

Amit Makashir

Amit is a Software Development Engineer on the Amazon Quick Suite visualization team, where he helped build Quick Sight’s layer maps and the geospatial mapping stack behind them. His work spans the mapping visuals customers see and the geocoding, data, and service infrastructure that power them. Drawn to maps, places, and spatial problem-solving, he brings that curiosity to much of his work. Outside the office, he enjoys the outdoors—hiking, exploring new destinations, and taking long scenic drives.

Jackson Dowden

Jackson is a Worldwide Generative AI Solutions Architect for Amazon Quick at AWS. He began at AWS as a Partner Solutions Architect and now focuses on helping ISV and healthcare & life sciences customers implement AI-driven analytics and embedded insights with the Quick service.

Koushik Muthanna Koravanda Ganapathy

Koushik is a Specialist Solutions Architect for Amazon Quick at AWS. He helps customers design, implement, and scale Quick across their organization, from architecture to everyday use.

Salim Khan

Salim is a Senior Worldwide Generative AI Solutions Architect for Amazon Quick at AWS. He has over 16 years of experience implementing enterprise business intelligence solutions. At AWS, Salim works with customers globally to design and implement AI-powered BI and generative AI capabilities on Amazon Quick. Prior to AWS, he worked as a BI consultant across industry verticals including Automotive, Healthcare, Entertainment, Consumer, Publishing, and Financial Services, delivering business intelligence, data warehousing, data integration, and master data management solutions.

item.title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
item.dc:creator: Subbu Dandamudi
item.description: Bayer Crop Science built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that lets breeders, analysts, and researchers ask natural language questions about their analytics platform. This post covers the ADE architecture, five design decisions, and how the team prepared it for production with AWS Unified Operations.
item.content:encoded:
Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls.

As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop.

ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models.

To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations. The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch.

Architecture overview

ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility. Amazon DynamoDB stores LangGraph checkpoint state. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL stores session records, user feedback, and analytics. Amazon ElastiCache caches agent responses with a time to live (TTL). Domain content in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and indexed in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Amazon CloudWatch captures runtime and application telemetry. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to agents as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code.

Figure 1: Agentic Decision Engine architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

ADE runs 22 specialist agents in production, each scoped to one domain with its own tools and data sources. For example, the Domain Expert Agent answers conceptual questions through RAG. The Operational Agent retrieves live workflow status and results from CDE. The Troubleshooting Agent analyzes operational telemetry. The Visualization Agent generates charts or returns existing dashboards. A customer-specific Models as Skill pattern converts model code and documentation into skill definitions stored in a central registry, so agents answer model-specific questions from the model’s implementation instead of generic model knowledge.

When a breeder asks, “Why did my phenotyping workflow fail yesterday?”, the supervisor classifies the intent and routes the request to the Troubleshooting Agent. That agent reads the workflow’s telemetry in CloudWatch and its status from the CDE API through AgentCore Gateway, identifies the failure point, and returns a diagnosis through the supervisor (Figure 2). The breeder doesn’t search logs directly. With the Troubleshooting Agent, a diagnosis that once took over an hour of manual log-hunting and waiting for engineer support now takes under 10 minutes.

Figure 2: ADE request flow: intent classification, cache lookup, specialist routing, and response

Five design decisions on the path to production

The Unified Operations TAM and DSE took part in the following decisions as members of the working team, not as an escalation point after the fact. That let Bayer test each design against AWS service behavior before committing to it, while keeping ownership of the architecture and the final call.

1. Externalize orchestration state without treating the runtime as stateless

AgentCore runtime provides isolated sessions that preserve execution context across invocations within a session’s lifecycle. That context isn’t a durable store for a multi-step workflow. ADE writes LangGraph checkpoints to DynamoDB so the graph can resume after scale-out events, restarts, or session boundaries without depending on one execution environment remaining available.

Principle: Use the runtime session for active execution, and persist the state required to resume or reconstruct the workflow in a durable service.

2. Separate enterprise identity, gateway access, and downstream authorization

Bayer standardizes on Microsoft Entra ID for user identity, while ADE’s services authorize each other with AWS-native mechanisms. Rather than force one token across every trust boundary, the team gave each boundary its own mechanism.

Entra ID remains the source of user identity. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authorizes service-to-service calls. AgentCore Gateway outbound authorization handles access to downstream CDE services. A request interceptor AWS Lambda function performs custom validation and passes the authorization attributes that downstream tools require. The team worked through the token contract at each hop with the DSE.

Principle: Identity failures in agent systems cluster at the transitions between user identity, agent identity, and tool identity. Define the issuer, audience, claims, scopes, and credential lifetime at every hop instead of reusing a token that is valid for one boundary at the next.

3. Treat model selection as an interface contract

During the build, the team evaluated a newer model version with reasoning mode enabled. For that version, the combination of tool use and structured output that ADE depends on was not compatible with how its agents were implemented. The DSE confirmed the constraint, and the team retained the current model for the release.

Principle: For tool-using agents, model choice is constrained by the full interface: tool calling, structured output, streaming behavior, reasoning features, latency, quota availability, and model-specific request semantics. A newer model is not automatically a drop-in replacement.

4. Control the tool surface before it controls the prompt

CDE manages more than 500 model configurations. A dedicated MCP server per API would have added deployment, authentication, and version management overhead. ADE instead registers OpenAPI specifications with AgentCore Gateway, which exposes the REST operations as MCP tools. Adding or changing an API becomes a schema and gateway configuration change instead of a new server deployment.

Tool schemas and descriptions also consume input tokens and compete with the user’s request and retrieved context. ADE scopes tools by specialist agent instead of giving every agent the full catalog. For larger catalogs, AgentCore Gateway supports semantic tool search, so an agent can find relevant tools without loading the entire catalog on every turn.

Principle: Scope the tool catalog per agent. Every tool definition adds tokens and widens the model’s decision space.

5. Promote complex capabilities from tools to agents

Visualization started as a tool invoked by other agents. As it grew, it needed its own data retrieval, chart selection logic, retries, error handling, and a decision about whether to generate a chart or return an existing dashboard. The team moved it into a specialist Visualization Agent. The agent generates on-demand charts with matplotlib and Plotly in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides a sandboxed code execution environment, and exchanges data with it through Amazon S3. When a prebuilt dashboard is the better answer, the agent returns the existing Amazon Quick or Power BI asset.

Principle: A tool performs a bounded operation. When a capability starts to own state, retries, planning, policy, or presentation decisions, model it as an agent.

Preparing ADE for production

As the build moved toward launch, the focus shifted from design to operability: detecting agent failures, attributing inference cost, and hardening the deployment.

Observability: Measure task failures, not only exceptions

A supervisor architecture turns one user request into a chain of model calls, tool calls, and agent handoffs. The final answer can be wrong even when every HTTP request succeeded. ADE encountered this directly: application exception handlers caught agent errors and returned responses that monitoring counted as successful. After reproducing the issue with the DSE, the team added custom CloudWatch metrics inside failure paths and alarms on agent-specific conditions: tool call errors, throttling, model timeouts, and structured output validation failures. Traces and invocation logs follow each request across the supervisor and specialists.

Principle: Distinguish transport success from task success. Agent observability should show whether the task completed, which agent or tool changed the outcome, and whether the response used the expected source.

Cost attribution: Combine billing attribution with request-level telemetry

One ADE request can invoke several models and tools, so account-level Amazon Bedrock spend doesn’t explain unit economics. The team designed the attribution approach with the DSE using three mechanisms that answer different questions. Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles attribute billed model usage to an application or workload. Request metadata and model invocation logging associate token usage with a specific agent, feature, or request. IAM principal attribution adds an identity dimension. Together they let the team estimate cost per interaction, identify expensive agents, and determine whether prompts, retrieved context, or tool definitions drive token use. In practice, the Visualization and Operational agents, which rely on MCP tools and multiple tool calls, consumed the most tokens.

The same telemetry surfaced a workload during launch preparation with a large repeated input prefix and no prompt cache activity. For supported models, placing stable instructions and tool definitions in a cacheable prompt prefix reduces repeated input processing, which lowers latency and token cost. For ADE, caching the stable prompt prefix cut input-token cost by 20–30 percent.

Security and launch readiness

IAM roles are scoped to each agent’s responsibility. The Troubleshooting Agent can read the operational data it needs for diagnosis but can’t modify workflows. The Domain Expert Agent can query its retrieval index but cannot call unrelated CDE APIs. In production today, ADE’s agent responses are governed by least privilege, read-only tool access scoped to each agent, structured output validation on agent responses, and answers grounded in retrieved CDE data and telemetry rather than open-ended generation. Bayer also plans to evaluate Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as an additional layer on these controls, complementing the custom safety checks already used in CDE multi-turn workflows.

Before launch, Unified Operations ran a Critical Workload Review and a Well-Architected review with the Generative AI Lens alongside the ADE team. Because the DSE already knew the workload, both reviews targeted ADE’s specific failure modes, capacity risks, and deployment gaps rather than generic best practices. Findings included gaps in failure visibility across the supervisor and specialist agents, mutable container image tags, limited image traceability, and missing vulnerability scanning. The team responded with stronger alarms, immutable versioned images, scan on push in Amazon ECR, and lifecycle policies for unused images.

The DSE also reviewed scaling and quota requirements with the team. Load testing validated both the application and its service quotas and exposed a networking failure mode that returned empty responses, which the team fixed before the production event. By launch, the team had tracked 35 blockers to resolution with Unified Operations.

Launch, operations, and next steps

Bayer launched ADE to a gated group rather than opening it to the whole organization at once. Since launch, more than 100 users across Bayer Crop Science have used ADE, including breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and engineers. Alongside its 22 specialist agents, ADE exposes about 20 API tools and can host third-party agents as it expands. Exposing those APIs through AgentCore Gateway rather than a dedicated server per API cut per-API integration overhead by more than 99 percent. In its first phase, ADE has resolved about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop.

CDE remains the governed execution layer for analytics. ADE adds a natural language layer over it, so users can ask about workflow status, results, model behavior, and failures without learning the location or interface of each underlying system.

The engagement then shifted from launch readiness to ongoing operations. The DSE continues to meet with the team, so issue triage and operational reviews start from existing knowledge of ADE instead of a new ramp-up. ADE’s critical CloudWatch alarms, including the agent-specific alarms described earlier, are onboarded to AWS Incident Detection and Response. When one fires, AWS Incident Management Engineers engage within 5 minutes and start from the workload’s context rather than from scratch. On the security side, AWS Security Incident Response engineers support the team during potential or active security events, so ADE has AWS monitoring and response coverage for both operational and security issues.

With agent-to-agent communication already in place, Bayer is focusing next on hybrid cloud agent interoperability. The team is exploring how agents running in different environments can discover and communicate with each other without manual configuration.

Conclusion

Bayer didn’t replace its analytics platform with ADE. It made CDE easier to query and operate. Most of the production work sat outside the prompts: durable state, identity boundaries, tool scoping, task-level observability, cost attribution, and launch readiness. Bayer owned the architecture and each of those decisions. Working with a designated DSE and TAM through AWS Unified Operations, the team tested those decisions against AWS service behavior during design and carried the same context into production.
